00.1Front Matter

Is book ke baare mein — MEAP Version 2 kya hai

Ye book RLHF — Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback — ki canonical reference banne ke liye likhi gayi hai. Matlab: ChatGPT jaise models ke peeche jo technique hai, woh andar se kaise kaam karti hai, uski poori kahani, formulas, recipes aur code — sab ek jagah.

Ye book kis ke liye hai

Ye book un logon ke liye hai jo samajhna chahte hain ki modern AI models kaise bante hain — researchers, engineers, aur woh log jo is field me job ya research project shuru karna chahte hain. Book ke teen maksad hain: pehla, badi tech companies ke andar chhupa cutting-edge research saaf topics aur trade-offs me samjhana; doosra, basic code examples se readers ke haath gande karwana — khud fine-tune karke dekhna; teesra, intuition dena ki RLHF modern AI ke liye itna crucial kyun hai.

Book ek baat saaf kar deti hai: RLHF ki ek exact recipe kisi ek need ke liye likhna impossible hai. Isi liye RLHF training as a service dene wali companies ki industry millions of dollars ki hai. Lekin jo reader ye knowledge le kar chalega, woh samay ke saath apni training khud karne ke aur kareeb aata jaayega.

MEAP Version 2 — is PDF me kya hai

Ye Manning Early Access Program (MEAP) Version 2 hai — Copyright 2026 Manning Publications. Is PDF me poore 18 chapters aur Appendix A (Definitions) hain, kul 246 pages. Is SPA me un sab ka poora content Hinglish me hai — har chapter, har formula, har recipe, har number.

Book ke teen hisse hain jinhe samajhna zaroori hai: Instruction Fine-tuning (Chapter 4), Reward Modeling (Chapter 5), aur Reinforcement Learning optimization (Chapter 6) — ye teeno mil kar classic RLHF pipeline banate hain. Uske baad reasoning, direct alignment, rejection sampling, preference data, synthetic data, tool use, regularization, over-optimization, evaluation aur product/UX aate hain.

Is SPA me kya hai: 18 chapters + Appendix A ka poora content Hinglish me — har formula, har table, har training recipe ke exact numbers, har figure — plus 8 interactive labs aur 36 interview FAQs. Jo kuch PDF me hai, woh sab yahan hai; jo PDF me nahi hai, woh invent nahi kiya gaya hai.

01.1Chapter 1 — Overview

Overview — RLHF kya hai aur kyun important hai

RLHF — Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback — ek technique hai jo human information ko AI systems me daalti hai. Ye un hard problems ko solve karne ke liye bani thi jahan sahi behaviour ko seedha likhna mushkil hai, kyunki insaan ki preferences aksar words me express hi nahi ho paati.

RLHF ka basic pipeline — 3 steps

  • Step 1 — Instruction-tuned model: pehle ek language model ko user ke sawaalon ka jawaab dena sikhaya jaata hai (Chapter 4).
  • Step 2 — Reward model: phir human preference data collect karke ek reward model train kiya jaata hai jo human preferences ko score karta hai (Chapter 5).
  • Step 3 — RL optimization: aakhir me language model ko ek RL optimizer se optimize kiya jaata hai — model generations sample karta hai aur reward model unhe rate karta hai (Chapter 6).

RLHF ki pehli breakthrough applications control problems aur traditional RL domains me thi, phir summarization, instructions follow karna, web information se question answering, aur "alignment" me use hua. ChatGPT ke release ke baad ye sabse zyada famous hua.

Post-training ke 3 optimization methods

Modern language model training me RLHF post-training ka ek component hai. Post-training ka matlab hai — downstream tasks ke liye models ko zyada useful banane ke techniques ka poora set. Ye teen optimization methods se summarize hota hai:

MethodKya karta haiKis baare me hai
1. Instruction / Supervised Fine-tuning (IFT/SFT)Formatting sikhata hai, instruction-following ki neev banata haiLanguage ke features seekhna
2. Preference Fine-tuning (PreFT)Human preferences se align karta hai, capabilities me chhota bump bhi deta haiLanguage ka style aur subtle human preferences jo quantify karna mushkil hai
3. Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards (RLVR)Verifiable domains me performance boost karta hai, zyada RL training seMaths/code jaise check karne layak tasks

RLHF dusre area — preference fine-tuning — ke andar rehta hai aur use dominate karta hai. Ye instruction tuning se zyada complex hai kyunki isme true objective ka ek proxy reward model hota hai aur data zyada noisy hota hai. Dusri taraf, ye RLVR se zyada established hai.

Ek aur important baat: language models train karna bahut complex process hai — aksar 10s se 100s logon ki badi technical teams aur data aur compute par millions of dollars lagte hain. Ye book isiliye hai ki readers ko woh tools milen jinse woh is field me jobs le saken aur research projects shuru kar saken.

Source: The RLHF Book, Manning, Chapter 1

01.2Chapter 1 — Overview

1.1 What Does RLHF Do? — base model vs post-trained model

Sabse bada sawaal — RLHF training models ko deta kya hai? Iska jawaab style aur format me chhupa hai: RLHF model ko yeh nahi sikhata ki kya bolna hai, yeh sikhata hai ki kaise bolna hai.

Base model kya karta hai — sirf sentence complete karta hai

Autoregressive pretraining ke end par ek language model sirf next token predict karta hai. Example: ek strong base model (405B parameters wala) ko prompt do — "The president of the united states in 2006 was" — to woh jawaab dene ke bajay sentence complete karta hai aur phir internet metadata jodta rehta hai: Florida ke governor, senators, executive orders, dates — sab kuch jo web par commonly uske aas-paas likha hota hai.

Uske opposite, wahi prompt post-trained model ko do to woh seedha jawaab deta hai: "George W. Bush was the president of the United States in 2006. He served two terms in office, from January 20, 2001, to January 20, 2009." Ye badlaav style ka hai — aur ye style post-training methods ka nateeja hai.

Style vs format — dono alag hain

  • Style: information present karne ka manner — tone. Example: presentation se pehle panic kar rahe user ko blunt style me jawaab do ("You'll be fine, practice karo, so jaao") vs warm supportive style me ("Ye stressful hai aur normal reaction hai — ek quick practice run karo, do points yaad rakho, phir rest karo"). Dono me information same hai, feel bilkul alag hai.
  • Format: jawaab ki structure. Early model simple jawaab deta hai ("same time par so jaao, caffeine avoid karo"). Modern model markdown, lists, headings aur sections ke saath rich jawaab deta hai — "Better sleep, in practice", phir "Tonight (quick wins)" aur "Daily basics (most impact)" jaise sections.

Instruction fine-tuning model ko question-answer format me reliably respond karna sikhata hai. RLHF uske baad un jawaabon ko reliable, warm aur engaging banata hai — wahi jawaab jo hum aaj models se expect karte hain.

RLHF ka mechanism — token-level nahi, response-level

Instruction fine-tuning per-token update karta hai: model ko sikhata hai ki dekhe hue examples ke kareeb text ke baad kaunsa specific token aana chahiye. RLHF response level par tune karta hai — poori response ko dekhta hai, aur model ko batata hai ki kaunsi response behtar hai, bina yeh bataye ki exact response kya honi chahiye. Aur RLHF negative feedback bhi deta hai — kaunsi response avoid karni hai. Is training ko contrastive loss function kehte hain, aur ye poori book me baar-baar aayega.

Research ne establish kiya hai ki RLHF instruction fine-tuning ke comparison me domains ke across zyada generalize karta hai — isiliye ye general-purpose models banane me madad karta hai.

Cost aur limitations — free nahi hai

Ye flexibility badi advantage hai, lekin implementation challenges bhi hain: reward model train karna padta hai jiske best practices strongly established nahi hain aur application area par depend karte hain; optimization over-optimization ka shikaar ho sakta hai kyunki reward signal best case me bhi ek proxy objective hai, isiliye regularization chahiye; aur RLHF ko strong starting point chahiye — ye har problem ka akela solution nahi hai. Isiliye RLHF implement karna simple instruction fine-tuning se zyada costly hai — compute, data cost aur time teeno me — aur unexpected challenges aate hain jaise length bias (lambi responses ko zyada reward milna).

Source: The RLHF Book, Manning, Chapter 1

01.3Chapter 1 — Overview

1.2 An Intuition for Post-Training — elicitation theory

Post-training itna powerful kyun hai? Book ka jawaab hai elicitation interpretation — post-training kuch naya nahi sikhata, woh base model ke andar pehle se maujood potential ko nikaal kar amplify karta hai.

Formula 1 analogy — chassis vs aerodynamics

Base model ko ek car ke chassis ki tarah samjho — chassis woh space define karta hai jiske aas-paas car banti hai. Formula 1 me teams saal ki shuruaat me naya chassis aur engine le kar aati hain, phir poora saal aerodynamics aur systems par kaam karti hain — aur car ki performance dramatically improve ho jaati hai. Best F1 teams season ke dauraan chassis-to-chassis badlaav se zyada improve karti hain.

Post-training ke saath bhi yahi hota hai: ek static base model se bahut performance nikali jaa sakti hai jab tum uski quirks aur tendencies samajhne lagte ho. Best post-training teams bahut kam time me bahut performance extract kar leti hain.

Concrete example — OLMoE: 35 se 48, pretraining badle bina

Ek achha example ek fully-open, chhote Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) model ka hai. Pehla version fall 2024 me release hua. Dusre version me sirf post-training update kiya gaya — pretraining ka zyada hissa same raha — aur popular benchmarks par evaluation average 35 se 48 ho gaya. Matlab 13 points ka jump, sirf post-training se.

Isi intuition ko book Elicitation Theory of Post-training kehti hai: base models me internet par pretraining se bahut latent potential hota hai, aur post-training ka kaam hai models ko next-token prediction se conversation question-answering me reshape karna, saath me woh saara knowledge aur intelligence extract karna.

Superficial Alignment Hypothesis — sahi intuition, galat conclusion

Isse juda idea Superficial Alignment Hypothesis hai, jo ek paper se aaya jiska naam hai "LIMA: Less is More for Alignment". Us paper ka claim tha: model ka knowledge aur capabilities lagbhag poori tarah pretraining me seekhe jaate hain, jabki alignment sirf ye sikhata hai ki users se interact karte waqt formats ka kaunsa subdistribution use karna hai. Agar ye hypothesis sahi hai, to ek pretrained model ko sirf kuch hazaar examples se sufficiently tune kiya jaa sakta hai.

Book kahti hai ye paper kuch important intuitions sahi pakad raha hai, lekin bade picture me galat reasons se. Haan, kuch hazaar instruction fine-tuning samples se model ko substantially change kiya jaa sakta hai aur narrow evaluations jaise AlpacaEval, MT Bench, ChatBotArena improve kiye jaa sakte hain — lekin ye challenging capabilities me hamesha translate nahi hota. Isi liye bade labs apne chat models ko sirf us dataset par train nahi karte.

Aur hypothesis isiliye bhi galat hai kyunki aaj ke base models (bina post-training ke) ko maths problems par reinforcement learning se train karke poora chain-of-thought reasoning output karna sikhaya jaa sakta hai, aur phir woh BigBenchHard, Zebra Logic, AIME jaise reasoning evaluations par zyada score karte hain. Post-training sirf "vibes" ke liye nahi hai — ye 2023 me field ko overcome karna pada ek lesson tha. Aaj style behaviour ke upar operate karta hai — jaise popular long chain of thought.

Source: The RLHF Book, Manning, Chapter 1

01.4Chapter 1 — Overview

1.3 How We Got Here — Alpaca se DPO tak ka safar

ChatGPT ke release ke baad se post-training kai seasons aur moods se guzra hai. Ye section woh timeline batata hai — kaise open recipes aage badhe, ruke, phir dobara toote.

Alpaca era — vibes ka benchmark

Shuruaat me Alpaca, Vicuna, Koala aur Dolly jaise models aaye — limited human datapoints aur Self-Instruct style synthetic data se original LLaMA ko normally fine-tune karke ChatGPT jaisa behaviour paane ki koshish. Un early models ka benchmark poori tarah "vibes" (aur human evaluation) tha — sab is baat se captivated the ki chhote models itne impressive behaviours dikha sakte hain. Excitement justified tha.

Open post-training closed counterparts se tez chal raha tha — zyada models, zyada noise. Companies scramble kar rahi thi, kuch merge ho rahi thi, aur follow-up me time lag raha tha. Phases aate rahe: open recipes surge karte, phir peeche reh jaate.

Doubt ka daur — "instruction tuning is enough"

Alpaca ke baad pehla lag aaya — skepticism aur doubt ka daur. Bahut si companies ko shak tha ki unhe RLHF ki zaroorat bhi hai. Ek common phrase bahut popular ho gaya tha — "instruction tuning is enough for alignment" — aur aaj bhi uska wazan hai, despite heavy obvious pressures against it.

Ye doubt khaas taur par open me raha, jahan groups ke paas $100K se $1M ke order ke data budgets nahi the. Jo companies ne RLHF early embrace kiya, woh jeet gayi. Ek lab ne 2022 tak RLHF par extensive research publish ki aur aaj uski post-training ko best mana jaata hai.

DPO era — May 2023

Open alignment methods me pehla shift Direct Preference Optimization (DPO) ki kahani thi — May 2023 me posted paper ne dikhaya ki RLHF wali optimization problem ko kam moving parts ke saath solve kiya jaa sakta hai, pairwise preference data par seedha gradient steps le kar. Shuru me koi clearly impactful DPO model nahi tha — ye badla jab breakthrough DPO models aaye, sab ek behtar, lower learning rate dhoondhne par contingent the. Zephyr-Beta, Tülu 2 aur kai models ne dikhaya ki DPO era shuru ho gaya hai.

Late 2023 se preference-tuning ek achhe model release karne ke liye table stakes ban gaya. DPO era 2024 tak chala — algorithm ke never-ending variants ke roop me — lekin open recipes phir slump me chale gaye, knowledge aur resources ki had tak saturate ho kar. Zephyr aur Tulu 2 ke ek saal baad bhi wahi breakout dataset, UltraFeedback, open recipes me preference tuning ke liye arguably ab bhi state-of-the-art hai.

Us dauraan Llama 3.1 aur Nemotron 4 340B reports ne substantive hints diye ki large-scale post-training bahut zyada complex aur impactful hai. Closed labs full post-training kar rahe hain — instruction tuning, RLHF, prompt design ka large multi-stage process — jabki academic papers sirf surface scratch kar rahe hain. Tülu 3 ne future academic post-training research ki neev rakhne ke liye ek comprehensive, open effort represent kiya.

Aaj post-training ek complex process hai — training objectives ko various orders me apply karke specific capabilities target ki jaati hain. Aane wale saalon me best practices emerge hongi ki unhe kaise interleave karna hai.

Source: The RLHF Book, Manning, Chapter 1
← Previous1.2 An Intuition for Post-Training — elicitation theoryNext →1.4 Future of RLHF — PreFT, DAA aur aage
01.5Chapter 1 — Overview

1.4 Future of RLHF — PreFT, DAA aur aage

Language modeling me investment ke saath traditional RLHF methods ke kai variations emerge hue. Aaj "RLHF" colloquially multiple overlapping approaches ka synonym ban gaya hai.

RLHF preference fine-tuning (PreFT) techniques ka ek subset hai. Isme Direct Alignment Algorithms (DAAs) bhi aate hain (Chapter 8) — woh methods jo DPO ke downstream hain aur preference learning problem ko preference data par seedha gradient steps le kar solve karte hain, bina intermediate reward model seekhe. RLHF woh tool hai jo language models ki "post-training" me rapid progress se sabse zyada associated hai — post-training ka matlab hai large-scale autoregressive training (primarily web data) ke baad ki saari training.

Jab fine-tuning language models with RL ke aur successes aate hain — jaise reasoning models (o1) — to RLHF ko woh bridge mana jaayega jisne large base models ko fine-tune karne ke liye RL methods me aur investment enable kiya. Saath me, jab spotlight near future me RLHF ke RL hisse par zyada intense hoga — valuable tasks par performance maximize karne ke tareeke ke roop me — tab bhi RLHF ka core wahi rahega: ye modern AI ke saamne khade grand problems ko study karne ka ek lens hai. Hum human values aur objectives ki complexities ko un systems me kaise map karen jise hum regular use karte hain? Ye book un problems par decades ke research aur lessons ki neev banne ki umeed rakhti hai.

Chapter 1 ka takeaway: RLHF ne base models ko sentence completers se helpful assistants me badla. Post-training ka kaam latent potential ko elicit karna hai — aur RLHF uska sabse established tool hai, lekin akela nahi: SFT, PreFT aur RLVR teeno mil kar modern post-training banate hain.
Source: The RLHF Book, Manning, Chapter 1

02.1Chapter 2 — A Tiny History of RLHF

Chapter 2 intro — A Tiny History of RLHF: teen eras

RLHF aur usse related methods bahut naye hain. Ye chapter history isiliye batata hai taaki dikhaya jaa sake ki procedures kitne recent formalize hue hain, aur kitna documentation academic literature me hai.

Chapter ka maksad ye stage set karna hai: RLHF bahut tezi se evolve ho raha hai, isiliye book kuch methods par uncertainty express karegi, aur expectation rakhegi ki kuch details kuch core practices ke aas-paas change ho sakti hain. Papers aur methods jo yahan list hain, woh dikhate hain ki RLHF pipeline ke pieces wahi kyun hain jo hain — kyunki kuch seminal papers to modern language models se bilkul alag applications ke liye the.

Ye chapter comprehensive review nahi hai — ye ek starting point aur retelling hai ki hum aaj yahan kaise pahunche. Focus intentionally recent work par hai jo ChatGPT tak le gaya. RL literature me preferences se seekhne par substantial aur kaam hai; exhaustive list ke liye ek proper survey paper use karna chahiye.

Teen eras — ek nazar me

EraPeriodKya hua
Origins2018 takRL on preferences — TAMER, COACH, Atari par trajectories se seekhna
Language models par RLHF2019–2022Summarization, InstructGPT, WebGPT, red teaming, Claude ke early versions
ChatGPT era2023–presentRLHF har leading model me; PreFT, DPO aur reasoning methods ka expansion
Source: The RLHF Book, Manning, Chapter 2

02.2Chapter 2 — A Tiny History of RLHF

2.1 Origins to 2018: RL on Preferences

Aaj ke techniques ki jadein early RL-from-preferences literature me hain — games aur robots par, language models par nahi.

TAMER aur COACH — humans se score karwana

Modern RLHF jaisa approach rakhne wale pehle papers me se ek TAMER tha — Training an Agent Manually via Evaluative Reinforcement. Isme humans agent ke actions ko iteratively score karte the, usse ek reward model seekha jaata tha, aur phir us reward model se action policy seekhi jaati thi. Uske aas-paas ya jald baad me ek actor-critic algorithm, COACH, aaya jahan human feedback (positive aur negative dono) advantage function ko tune karne ke liye use hota tha.

2017 — Atari trajectories par RLHF

Primary reference 2017 ka ek paper hai jisme RLHF ko Atari games ke andar agents ki trajectories ke beech preferences par apply kiya gaya. Ye kaam ek lab ke Deep Q-Networks (DQN) par seminal work ke jald baad aaya, jisne dikhaya tha ki RL agents popular video games scratch se seekh kar solve kar sakte hain. Paper ne dikhaya ki kuch domains me trajectories ke beech humans ka choose karna environment se seedha interact karne se zyada effective ho sakta hai.

Is method ko aur direct reward modeling se expand kiya gaya, aur early RLHF work me deep learning ka adoption TAMER ke ek neural network extension se ek saal baad cap hua. Ye era transition karne laga jab reward models ko ek general notion ke roop me propose kiya gaya — sirf RL problems solve karne ka tool nahi, balki alignment study karne ka method.

Source: The RLHF Book, Manning, Chapter 2
← PreviousChapter 2 intro — A Tiny History of RLHF: teen erasNext →2.2 2019 to 2022: RL from Human Preferences on Language Models
02.3Chapter 2 — A Tiny History of RLHF

2.2 2019 to 2022: RL from Human Preferences on Language Models

GPT-2 (2018) aur GPT-3 (2020) ke beech, RLHF ko AI labs ne tezi se adopt kiya jo large language models scale kar rahe the.

2019 — modern RLHF ka template

2019 ka sabse pehla kaam, "Fine-Tuning Language Models from Human Preferences", modern RLHF se bahut striking similarities rakhta hai. Kai canonical terms usi paper me formalize hue: reward models seekhna, regularization ke liye Kullback-Leibler divergence (KL divergence), feedback diagrams, aur aise hi. Bas final models ke evaluation tasks aur capabilities aaj se alag the.

Kahan-kahan apply hua

  • General summarization — human feedback se summarize karna seekhna
  • Books ki recursive summarization — lambi books ko hissa-hissa summarize karna
  • Instruction following (InstructGPT) — instructions follow karna sikhana
  • Browser-assisted question-answering (WebGPT) — web browse karke jawaab dena
  • Citations ke saath answers (GopherCite) — verified quotes se answers support karna
  • General dialogue (Sparrow) — targeted human judgements se dialogue agents ko align karna

Seminal areas jo future define karte hain

  • Reward model over-optimization: RL optimizers ka preference data par train kiye gaye models ko over-fit karne ki ability
  • Language models as alignment study: ek general language assistant ko alignment ke laboratory ke roop me dekhna
  • Red teaming: language model ki safety assess karne ka process

Kaam chat models par RLHF refine karne par jaari raha. Ek lab ne early Claude versions ke liye iska extensively use kiya, aur early RLHF open-source tools emerge hue — jinme RL frameworks aur libraries shaamil the.

Source: The RLHF Book, Manning, Chapter 2
← Previous2.1 Origins to 2018: RL on PreferencesNext →2.3 2023 to Present: ChatGPT Era
02.4Chapter 2 — A Tiny History of RLHF

2.3 2023 to Present: ChatGPT Era

ChatGPT ki announcement me RLHF ki role bilkul saaf thi: "We trained this model using Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback (RLHF), using the same methods as InstructGPT, but with slight differences in the data collection setup."

Uske baad se RLHF leading language models me extensively use hua hai. Ye use hona well known hai: Constitutional AI wale assistant me, Llama 2 aur Llama 3 me, Nemotron me, Tülu 3 me, aur aur bhi kai models me.

Aaj — RLHF se aage, preference fine-tuning (PreFT)

Aaj RLHF ek broader field — preference fine-tuning — me grow ho raha hai, jisme naye applications hain:

  • Process reward — intermediate reasoning steps ke liye reward (Chapter 5)
  • Direct alignment algorithms — DPO se inspired methods (Chapter 8)
  • Execution feedback se seekhna — code ya maths se feedback, aur reasoning methods jo o1 se inspired hain (Chapter 7)
Chapter 2 ka takeaway: RLHF 2008 ke TAMER se 2017 ke Atari experiments se hote hue 2019 me language models par aaya, aur 2022 ke end me ChatGPT ke saath mainstream ban gaya. Har era ne pipeline ka ek piece formalize kiya — reward model, KL regularization, preference data, red teaming — jo aaj bhi use hote hain.
Source: The RLHF Book, Manning, Chapter 2
← Previous2.2 2019 to 2022: RL from Human Preferences on Language ModelsNext →3.1 Problem Formulation — RL ka standard setup
03.1Chapter 3 — Training Overview

3.1 Problem Formulation — RL ka standard setup

RLHF ka optimization standard RL setup ke upar banta hai. Is section me woh setup — states, actions, rewards, trajectories — aur phir RLHF ke liye uska simplified version hai.

Standard RL — agent, state, action, reward

RL me ek agent actions at leta hai, jo ek policy π(at | st) se sample hote hain, environment ke state st ko dekh kar, reward r(st, at) maximize karne ke liye. Environment transition dynamics p(st+1 | st, at) ke hisaab se evolve hota hai, initial state distribution ρ0(s0) se shuru ho kar.

Policy aur dynamics mil kar ek trajectory distribution banate hain:

Equation 3.1 — Trajectory distribution: pπ(τ) = ρ0(s0) × Πt=0..T-1 π(at|st) × p(st+1|st, at). Yahan τ ek trajectory hai — states, actions aur rewards ka poora sequence: τ = (s0, a0, r0, s1, a1, r1, …, sT, aT, rT).

Finite episode me, horizon T ke saath, RL agent ka goal ye optimization solve karna hai:

Equation 3.2 — RL objective: J(π) = Eτ~pπ[ Σt=0..T-1 γt × r(st, at) ]. Yahan γ (gamma) discount factor hai, 0 se 1 ke beech, jo near rewards vs future rewards ko balance karta hai. Continuing tasks ke liye T → ∞ liya jaata hai aur discounting (γ < 1) objective ko well-defined rakhta hai.

Example — CartPole (inverted pendulum)

Transition function ko concrete karne ke liye classic CartPole task dekho:

  • State (st): cart ki position/velocity aur pole ka angle/angular velocity — st = (xt, ẋt, θt, θ̇t).
  • Action (at): cart par left/right horizontal force lagana, at ∈ {−F, +F}.
  • Reward (rt): har step par r = 1 jab tak pole balanced rahe aur cart track par rahe (jaise |xt| ≤ 2.4 aur |θt| ≤ 12°). Episode terminate ho jaata hai jab koi bound violate ho.
  • Dynamics: kai environments me dynamics deterministic hote hain (p ek point mass hai) aur st+1 = f(st, at) ke roop me Euler integration se likhe jaa sakte hain, step size Δt ke saath. Constants: cart mass mc, pole mass mp, pole half-length l, gravity g.

Ye general setup ka concrete instance hai: policy action chunti hai, transition function state ko aage badhata hai, aur reward episode bhar accumulate hota hai.

Source: The RLHF Book, Manning, Chapter 3
← Previous2.3 2023 to Present: ChatGPT EraNext →3.1.2–3.1.4 — RL se RLHF: kya badla, KL penalty
03.2Chapter 3 — Training Overview

3.1.2–3.1.4 — RL se RLHF: kya badla, KL penalty

RLHF ke liye standard RL setup ko language models ke hisaab se modify kiya jaata hai. Teen core changes hain — aur uske baad fine-tuning regime me regularization ki zaroorat padti hai.

Teen core changes — Table 3.1

AspectStandard RLRLHF (language models)
Reward signalEnvironment reward function r(st, at)Learned reward / preference model rθ(x, y) — prompt x, completion y
State transitionYes: dynamics p(st+1 | st, at)Typically no: prompts x dataset se sample hote hain; completion next prompt define nahi karta
ActionSingle environment action atEk completion y (tokens ka sequence) jo πθ(·|x) se sample hoti hai
Reward granularityOften per-step / fine-grainedUsually response-level (bandit-style) poori completion par
HorizonMulti-step episode (T > 1)Often single-step (T = 1), haan multi-turn ko longer-horizon ke roop me model kiya jaa sakta hai

In changes ka matlab: pehla, reward function ki jagah human preferences ka ek learned model use hota hai — isse designer ko flexibility aur final results par control zyada milta hai, lekin implementation complexity ki keemat par. Dusra, state transitions nahi hote — initial states prompts hote hain jo training dataset se sample hote hain, aur "action" us prompt ka completion hota hai; ye action next state ko impact nahi karta, sirf reward model se score hota hai. Teesra, reward attribution poori sequence ke liye hoti hai — multiple generated tokens ka ek bandit problem.

Single-turn nature ki wajah se optimization ko time horizon aur discount factor ke bina rewrite kiya jaa sakta hai:

Equation 3.3 — RLHF objective (simplified): J(π) = Eτ~π[ rθ(st, at) ]. Kai tareekon se, RLHF RL optimizers se heavily inspired hai, lekin actual implementation traditional RL se bahut distinct hai.

Fine-tuning aur regularization — KL penalty

Traditional RL problems me agent randomly initialized policy se seekhta hai, lekin RLHF me hum ek strong pretrained base model se shuru karte hain jiske paas pehle se bahut capabilities hain. Ye strong prior ek zaroorat paida karta hai: optimization ko initial policy se zyada door drift karne se rokna. Isiliye RLHF techniques multiple types ki regularization use karte hain.

Sabse common change optimization function me ek distance penalty add karna hai — current RLHF policy aur optimization ke starting point (reference policy πref) ke beech ka difference:

Equation 3.4 — KL-regularized objective: J(π) = Eτ~π[ rθ(st, at) ] − β × DKL(πRL(·|st) ∥ πref(·|st)). Yahan DKL Kullback-Leibler divergence hai — jo measure karta hai ki ek probability distribution dusre se kitni alag hai: DKL(P∥Q) = Ex~P[ log P(x) − log Q(x) ]. Ye RL policy ko reference se zyada door jaane par penalize karta hai.

Is formulation me bahut saari RLHF training research is baat par hai ki ek certain "KL budget" ko kaise spend karna hai — initial model se distance ke roop me measure kiya gaya. Details Chapter 15 (Regularization) me hain.

Optimization tools — is book me kya seekhoge

  • Reward modeling (Chapter 5): preference data se signal capture karke ek scalar reward output karne wala model.
  • Instruction fine-tuning (Chapter 4): RLHF ka prerequisite — models ko question-answer format sikhana.
  • Rejection sampling (Chapter 9): sabse basic RLHF technique — reward model se filter karke instruction fine-tuning ke liye candidate completions chunna.
  • Policy gradients (Chapter 6): RL algorithms jo reward model ke signal se language model ke parameters update karte hain.
  • Direct alignment algorithms (Chapter 8): pairwise preference data se seedha policy optimize karna, bina intermediate reward model ke.

Modern RLHF-trained models hamesha instruction fine-tuning ke baad inme se ek mixture use karte hain.

Source: The RLHF Book, Manning, Chapter 3
← Previous3.1 Problem Formulation — RL ka standard setupNext →3.2 Canonical Training Recipes — InstructGPT, Tülu 3, DeepSeek R1
03.3Chapter 3 — Training Overview

3.2 Canonical Training Recipes — InstructGPT, Tülu 3, DeepSeek R1

Samay ke saath kuch models canonical recipes ban gaye — ye recipes us samay ki data practices aur model abilities ko reflect karte hain. Jaise recipes purani hoti hain, waisi characteristics wale models train karna aasan ho jaata hai aur kam data lagta hai. General trend hai: zyada optimization steps, zyada training algorithms, zyada diverse datasets aur evaluations.

InstructGPT — classic 3-step recipe

ChatGPT ke aane ke samay, widely accepted ("canonical") post-training method ke teen major steps the, RLHF central piece ke saath. Base language model (large-scale web text par train kiya hua next-token prediction model) ke upar:

  • Step 1: ~10K examples par instruction tuning — model ko question-answer format follow karna sikhana, primarily human-written data se basic skills ke saath.
  • Step 2: ~100K pairwise prompts par reward model train karna — ye model instruction-tuned checkpoint se train hota hai aur diverse values capture karta hai jo final training me chahiye. Reward model hi RLHF ka optimization target hai.
  • Step 3: ~100K prompts par instruction-tuned model ko RLHF se train karna — model reward model ke against optimize hota hai, prompts ke set par generations karke ratings paane se pehle.

Tülu 3 — modern multi-stage recipe

Modern post-training me bahut zyada model versions aur training stages hote hain (Llama 2 ke liye documented 5 RLHF steps se bhi zyada). Leading models jaise ChatGPT ya Claude (circa 2025) me training ke kai iterative rounds hote hain — isme specialized models train karke unke weights merge karna bhi shaamil ho sakta hai taaki final model kai subtasks par capable ho.

Tülu 3 ek fully open example hai is multi-stage post-training ka, jisme RLHF major role play karta hai. Recipe ke teen stages:

StageDataKya karta hai
1. Instruction tuning~1M examplesPrimarily synthetic data, frontier models (jaise GPT-4o aur Llama 3.1 405B) ke mix se — general instruction following sikhata hai, mathematics ya coding jaise capabilities ki neev
2. On-policy preference data~1M preference pairsModel ki chattiness substantially boost karta hai (jaise ChatBotArena ya AlpacaEval 2) aur instruction tuning stage wali skills bhi improve karta hai
3. RL with Verifiable Rewards~10K promptsChhota RL run jo core skills jaise mathematics boost karta hai, overall performance maintain rakhte hue — modern reasoning models (jaise DeepSeek R1) ka precursor

Ye recipe Llama 3.1, OLMo 2 aur SmolLM models par successfully apply ki gayi hai.

DeepSeek R1 — reasoning models ki recipe

Reasoning language models (jaise o1) ke rise ke saath post-training best practices phir evolve hui — training stages ko re-order aur redistribute kiya gaya. Reasoning model post-training recipe ka clearest documentation DeepSeek R1 hai, jise bade Qwen 3 models (sirf 32B aur 225B MoE models) aur MiMo 7B ne mirror kiya hai:

  • Step 1 — "Cold-start" 100K+ on-policy reasoning samples: ye data ek earlier RL checkpoint (R1-Zero) se sample kiya gaya aur heavily filter kiya gaya, taaki model me ek specific reasoning process instill ho. "Cold-start" ka matlab hai RL ko little supervised data se seekhna.
  • Step 2 — Large-scale RL training: reasoning problems par model ke saath baar-baar RLVR chalana, "until convergence", variety of benchmarks par.
  • Step 3 — Rejection sampling: 3/4 reasoning problems aur 1/4 general queries par, general-purpose model me transition shuru karne ke liye.
  • Step 4 — Mixed RL training: reasoning problems (verifiable rewards) par general preference tuning reward models ke saath, model ko polish karne ke liye.

Is recipe ke evolutions hain, khaas taur par steps 3 aur 4 me, model ko users ke saamne laane se pehle finalize karne ke liye. Kai models tailored instruction datasets se shuru karte hain — chain-of-thought sequences jo existing models se heavily filter aur polish ki gayi hain — jo SFT alone se strong behaviours tak fast step deti hain, RL par jaane se pehle.

Chapter 3 ka takeaway: RLHF standard RL ka simplified version hai — no state transitions, response-level (bandit) rewards, aur KL penalty se reference policy ke kareeb rehna. Recipes evolve hui hain: InstructGPT ke ~10K/~100K/~100K se Tülu 3 ke ~1M/~1M/~10K tak, aur phir DeepSeek R1 ke reasoning-first order tak.
Source: The RLHF Book, Manning, Chapter 3
← Previous3.1.2–3.1.4 — RL se RLHF: kya badla, KL penaltyNext →Chapter 4 intro — Instruction Fine-tuning: RLHF ki neev
04.1Chapter 4 — Instruction Fine-tuning

Chapter 4 intro — Instruction Fine-tuning: RLHF ki neev

Early large pretrained language models next-token prediction objective se train hote the, aur by default unke paas instructions follow karne ka koi explicit interface nahi tha. Instruction fine-tuning ne ye badla — model ko text continue karne ke bajay instruction-response format me respond karna sikhaya.

Do lines of work ka convergence

Instruction fine-tuning tab takeoff hua jab do trends mile. Pehla, NLP bespoke task-specific fine-tuning se ek unified "text-to-text" ya instruction framing ki taraf shift hua — diverse datasets ko standardize karna aur ek hi model ko kai tasks par train karna straightforward ho gaya. Prominent examples: T5 models (unified text-to-text transformer), FLAN dataset (finetuned LMs are zero-shot learners), T0 models (multitask prompted training), aur Natural Instructions dataset (crowdsourcing instructions se cross-task generalization).

Doosra, pretrained LMs scale hue aur prompting/in-context learning ne dikhaya ki ek hi model kai tasks par generalize kar sakta hai — lekin woh generalization far zyada reliable ho jaata hai jab model ko instruction-response examples par explicitly train kiya jaaye. Dono trends mil kar instruction fine-tuning (IFT), ya supervised fine-tuning (SFT), ka era le aaye — jisme general models train karna wider audiences ke liye accessible ho gaya.

IFT aaj standard practice hai har language modeling pipeline me. Ye RLHF ki neev hai: ye model ko question-answering format ke liye taiyaar karta hai, aur ye pehla tool hai jo modern techniques ko naye domains me apply karne wale log istemal karte hain. Basic instruction-following abilities ke bina is book ki zyada tar pipelines — preference data collection se le kar online RLHF optimization tak — perform hi nahi ki jaa sakti.

Source: The RLHF Book, Manning, Chapter 4
← Previous3.2 Canonical Training Recipes — InstructGPT, Tülu 3, DeepSeek R1Next →4.1 Chat templates aur instructions ki structure
04.2Chapter 4 — Instruction Fine-tuning

4.1 Chat templates aur instructions ki structure

Post-training process ki shuruaat user queries ko format karne ka pattern define karne se hoti hai, taaki language model (jo information ko tokenizer se process karta hai) use aasani se padh sake.

Base model ke sirf kuch tokens

Pretrained language model ko prompt karna simple hai — model sirf kuch tokens jaanta hai: beginning-of-sequence token (jaise <bos_token>), end-of-sequence token (jaise <eos_token>), aur padding token (batches me khaali components manage karne ke liye). Base model ko prompt karne ke liye user tokens ka ek sequence deta hai jise model continue karta hai, jaise: <bos_token> The capital of the United States is — phir model tokens generate karta hai jab tak context window khatm na ho ya end-of-sequence token generate na ho jaaye.

Saare post-training stages — instruction tuning se le kar RLHF tak — isi formatting par rely karte hain. Jo tool user ke saath interaction ki structure handle karta hai, use chat template kehte hain.

ChatML template — Jinja code ka example

Book ek example deti hai — Jinja code jo Python me messages aur roles ki list ko tokens me transform karta hai. Template ye karta hai: system message ho to offset set karta hai, phir bos_token emit karta hai, phir har message ko serialize karta hai — role alternation enforce karte hue (system), user, assistant, user, assistant… — har message ko special tokens se wrap karta hai: <|im_start|><role> + content + <|im_end|> . Aakhir me agar generation prompt chahiye ho to <|im_start|>assistant append karta hai taaki model assistant role se generate karna shuru kare.

Teen roles — system, user, assistant

  • system: sirf conversation ke pehle message me use hota hai; agent ke liye instructions rakhta hai jo user ko dikhayi ya di nahi jaati — jaise date aur time, ya behaviours patch karna. Fun example: model ko batana "You are a friendly chatbot who always responds in the style of a pirate."
  • user: AI use karne wale insaan ke messages.
  • assistant: model ke responses (jo AI assistant ke roop me engage ho raha hai).

Example query "How many helicopters can a human eat in one sitting?" par token sequence aisa dikhta hai: system message, phir user message, phir <|im_start|>assistant — aur wahi final tokens model ko batate hain ki generate karna hai jab tak end-of-sequence token (<|im_end|>) na aa jaaye. Multi-turn me bhi yahi pattern extend hota hai — har turn <|im_start|> aur <|im_end|> se wrap hota hai.

Open ecosystem me standard method ye hai ki Jinja code tokenizer me save kiya jaata hai, apply_chat_template ke roop me. Upar wala template Chat Markup Language (ChatML) ka derivative hai — message formatting standardize karne ki ek early koshish. Aaj model providers hierarchical system use karte hain jahan user system message configure kar sakta hai, lekin kuch higher-level instructions user ko reveal ho bhi sakti hain aur nahi bhi.

Aur templates — Zephyr aur Tülu

Kai aur chat templates exist karte hain. Zephyr ka template <|system|>, <|user|>, <|assistant|> tokens use karta hai, har message ke end me </s> ke saath. Tülu ka template <|user|> aur <|assistant|> use karta hai, assistant response ke end me <|endoftext|> ke saath. Inke alawa, kai templates me tool-use jaise tasks ke liye formatting aur tokens hote hain.

Source: The RLHF Book, Manning, Chapter 4
← PreviousChapter 4 intro — Instruction Fine-tuning: RLHF ki neevNext →4.2 Best practices of instruction tuning
04.3Chapter 4 — Instruction Fine-tuning

4.2 Best practices of instruction tuning

Instruction tuning helpful language models banane ki neev ke roop me well-established hai. Successful instruction tuning ke kai tareeke hain — lekin kuch principles stable rehte hain.

  • High-quality data hi performance ki key hai. Completions woh hain jinse model asal me seekhta hai — kai cases me prompts predict nahi kiye jaate, isiliye model prompts predict karna nahi seekhta.
  • ~1M prompts se ek aisa model banaya jaa sakta hai jo excellent RLHF aur post-training ke capable ho. Aage scaling se bhi madad milti hai, lekin returns jaldi diminish hone lagte hain.
  • Best prompts woh hain jo downstream tasks ke distribution ke similar hon.
  • Agar instruction tuning ke baad multiple stages hain, to models process me kuch noise se recover kar sakte hain. Overall optimization ko optimize karna har individual stage se zyada important hai.

Data scale ki kahani bhi interesting hai: ChatGPT ke release ke turant baad, sirf 10K samples wale human datasets (jaise No Robots) state-of-the-art the. Saalon baad, zyada tar tasks par large-scale synthetic datasets best kaam karte hain. Narrow domains me — jaise chat alignment, bina maths ya code jaise hard skills ke — chhote, focused datasets bhi strong performance de sakte hain. Aur efficient fine-tuning (jaise model parameters ke kuch hisse ko quantize karke) training ko bahut accessible bana deti hai.

Source: The RLHF Book, Manning, Chapter 4
← Previous4.1 Chat templates aur instructions ki structureNext →4.3 Implementation — batch size, masking, loss
04.4Chapter 4 — Instruction Fine-tuning

4.3 Implementation — batch size, masking, loss

Loss function pretraining wali hi hai, lekin implementation me kuch key details alag hain. Ye details hi decide karti hain ki instruction tuning sahi tareeke se ho.

Chhote batch sizes

Pretraining ke comparison me instruction tuning (aur doosri post-training techniques jaise preference fine-tuning) substantially chhote batch sizes use karti hain. Example: OLMo 2 pretraining me 7B model ke liye 1024 sequences aur 13B ke liye 2048 sequences ka batch size use karta hai, jabki post-training me dono sirf 256 sequences ka batch use karte hain. Chhote batch sizes ka matlab hai ki training jobs ko pretraining jitne devices par shard nahi kiya jaa sakta — distributed setups me minimum per-device batch sizes hote hain, isiliye chhota global batch rakhne ke liye cumulatively kam GPUs use kar sakte ho. Practically ye limiting factor nahi hai kyunki SFT ke training token counts pretraining se bahut chhote hote hain, aur best final performance ke liye post-training me multiple seeds par training chahiye hoti hai.

Prompt masking — model sirf responses seekhe

Pretraining me batch ke har token ko autoregressively predict kiya jaata hai aur loss sab par apply hota hai. Instruction tuning me prompt tokens mask out kar diye jaate hain taaki model user queries ko accurately predict karna na seekhe — sirf responses seekhe. Yehi baat doosri post-training algorithms par bhi apply hoti hai.

Multi-turn masking — 2 common choices

  • (1) Final-turn only: sirf final assistant turn ke tokens loss me include hote hain, saara earlier context (earlier assistant turns samet) masked hota hai. Lambi conversations ko multiple training samples me "unroll" kiya jaa sakta hai: N turns wali conversation ke liye har example ek assistant response predict karta hai, saara prior context mask karke (aur future turns exclude karke).
  • (2) Mask user turns only: saare user turns masked hote hain, lekin har assistant turn loss me include hota hai. Yahan bhi unroll kar sakte ho agar zyada (chhote) training examples chahiye, lekin key difference ye hai ki intermediate assistant replies par seedha train kiya jaata hai.

Same loss function as pretraining: instruction tuning wahi autoregressive loss function use karti hai jo pretraining me use hoti hai — lekin substantially different data aur masking ke saath (full sequences par train karna, jabki pretraining documents batches me split ho sakte hain).

Chapter 4 ka takeaway: IFT RLHF ka prerequisite hai — chat template (system/user/assistant roles) format define karta hai, prompt masking model ko sirf responses sikhata hai, aur ~1M high-quality prompts ek strong starting point dete hain. Batch sizes chhote hote hain (OLMo 2: 256 vs 1024/2048), lekin token counts bhi chhote hote hain.
Source: The RLHF Book, Manning, Chapter 4
← Previous4.2 Best practices of instruction tuningNext →Chapter 5 intro — Reward Modeling: preferences ko score me badlo
05.1Chapter 5 — Reward Modeling

Chapter 5 intro — Reward Modeling: preferences ko score me badlo

Reward models modern RLHF ke core hain — ye woh jagah hai jahan complex human preferences seekhi jaati hain. Ye complex features ko data se compress karke ek representation me badal dete hain jo downstream training me use ho sake.

Reward models RL research me historically environment rewards ke proxy ke roop me extensively use hote rahe hain. Modern form me inhe value alignment problem study karne ka tool propose kiya gaya tha. Ye models kisi input ko le kar ek single scalar value of reward output karte hain. Traditional RL problems me ye environment reward ko approximate karne ki koshish karte the, lekin RLHF me reward models asal me ek probability output karte hain — ki ek input "high quality" hai (yaani pairwise preference relation me chosen answer hai).

Reward modeling ki practice inverse reinforcement learning se closely related hai — jahan problem hai agent ki reward function ko uske behaviour ki trajectories se approximate karna — aur deep RL ke doosre areas se bhi. High-level problem statement same hai, lekin implementation aur focus areas bilkul alag hain, isiliye inhe aksar totally separate areas mana jaata hai.

Is chapter me x prompts ko aur y completions ko denote karta hai — ye notation language model literature me common hai, jahan methods individual tokens ke bajay full prompt-completion pairs par operate karte hain.

Sabse common reward model, jise Bradley-Terry reward model kehte hain aur jo is chapter ka primary focus hai, ye predict karta hai ki ek piece of text training comparisons me "preferred" piece ke kareeb tha. Baad me iski comparison Outcome Reward Models (ORMs), Process Reward Models (PRMs) aur doosre types se ki gayi hai.

Source: The RLHF Book, Manning, Chapter 5
← Previous4.3 Implementation — batch size, masking, lossNext →5.1 Training Reward Models — Bradley-Terry model
05.2Chapter 5 — Reward Modeling

5.1 Training Reward Models — Bradley-Terry model

Reward model ka canonical implementation Bradley-Terry model of preference se derive hota hai. Standard reward model train karne ke do popular expressions hain — dono mathematically equivalent hain.

Bradley-Terry — pairwise preference ki probability

Bradley-Terry model define karta hai ki do items i aur j ke beech pairwise comparison me judge i ko j par prefer karne ki probability kya hai:

Equation 5.1: P(i > j) = pi / (pi + pj). Model assume karta hai ki har item ki ek latent strength pi > 0 hoti hai, aur observed preferences in underlying strengths ka noisy reflection hote hain.

Unbounded scores se reparametrize karna common hai, jahan pi = eri:

Equation 5.2: P(i > j) = eri / (eri + erj) = σ(ri − rj), jahan σ sigmoid function hai: σ(z) = 1 / (1 + e−z). Sirf scores ke differences matter karte hain: saare ri me same constant add karne se P(i > j) unchanged rehta hai. Ye forms nature ka law nahi hain — human preferences ka ek useful approximation hai jo RLHF me aksar achha kaam karta hai.

Loss function — chosen vs rejected

Reward model train karne ke liye ek loss function chahiye jo upar wale relation ko satisfy kare. Practically, ye language model ko ek aise model me convert karke kiya jaata hai jo ek scalar score output karta hai — aksar ek chhote linear head se jo ek single logit produce karta hai. Prompt x aur do sampled completions y1 aur y2 diye jaaye, to dono ko reward model rθ se score kiya jaata hai: rθ(yi|x).

Equation 5.3: P(y1 > y2|x) = exp(rθ(y1|x)) / (exp(rθ(y1|x)) + exp(rθ(y2|x))). Preferred completion ko yc (chosen) aur rejected ko yr kehte hain, jahan yc ≻ yr ka matlab hai yc, yr se preferred hai.

Is function ki log-likelihood maximize karke (ya negative log-likelihood minimize karke) reward model train karne ka loss milta hai:

Equation 5.5 (pehla form): L(θ) = −log(σ(rθ(yc|x) − rθ(yr|x)))
Equation 5.6 (doosra form): L(θ) = log(1 + erθ(yr|x) − rθ(yc|x))
Dono equivalent hain: Δ = rθ(yc|x) − rθ(yr|x) rakh kar aur σ(Δ) = 1/(1+e−Δ) use kar ke, −log σ(Δ) = log(1 + e−Δ) milta hai. Dono forms RLHF literature me dikhte hain.
Source: The RLHF Book, Manning, Chapter 5
← PreviousChapter 5 intro — Reward Modeling: preferences ko score me badloNext →5.2–5.3 Architecture aur Implementation Example (PyTorch)
05.3Chapter 5 — Reward Modeling

5.2–5.3 Architecture aur Implementation Example (PyTorch)

Reward model implement karna conceptually simple hai — asli complexity data loader aur inference pipeline setup karne me hai.

Architecture — linear head, ek scalar

Reward models implement karne ka sabse common tareeka Transformer ke AutoModelForSequenceClassification jaisa abstraction hai — language model ke upar ek chhota linear head append kar diya jaata hai jo do outcomes — chosen aur rejected — ke beech classification karta hai. Inference time par model ek single logit output karta hai: probability ki text chosen hai. Doosre options bhi hain, jaise final embeddings se seedha ek linear layer lena, lekin open tooling me woh kam common hain.

Loss — sirf 1 line

Sahi dataloader (tokenized, chosen aur rejected prompts + completions) mil jaaye to loss implement karna bahut simple hai:

import torch.nn as nn
# inputs_chosen / inputs_rejected me prompt tokens x aur respective
# completion tokens (y_c ya y_r) hote hain, jinhe reward model jointly score karta hai.
rewards_chosen = model(**inputs_chosen)
rewards_rejected = model(**inputs_rejected)

loss = -nn.functional.logsigmoid(rewards_chosen - rewards_rejected).mean()

Poora model class — BradleyTerryRewardModel

Model structure: ek causal language model jiske upar ek head add kiya gaya hai jo final hidden state se input ka score banata hai. Key detail: sequence representation ke liye last non-padding token (EOS token) ki hidden state li jaati hai — attention_mask se lengths nikaal kar. Code me _sequence_rep yehi karta hai: lengths = attention_mask.sum(dim=1) - 1, phir hidden[batch_idx, lengths], phir self.head(seq_repr).squeeze(-1) se ek scalar reward per sequence milta hai.

Ek important practice: reward models train karte waqt sabse common practice hai sirf 1 epoch train karna, overfitting se bachne ke liye. Aur implementation complexity ka zyada hissa data-loaders ko sahi tareeke se construct karne aur distributed learning systems ke aas-paas hota hai.

Source: The RLHF Book, Manning, Chapter 5
← Previous5.1 Training Reward Models — Bradley-Terry modelNext →5.4 Variants — margin loss, balancing, K-wise loss
05.4Chapter 5 — Reward Modeling

5.4 Variants — margin loss, balancing, K-wise loss

Reward modeling RLHF ka relatively under-explored area hai. Traditional loss ko kai popular works me modify kiya gaya hai, lekin modifications kisi ek best practice me solidify nahi hue hain.

Preference Margin Loss — Likert scale ka magnitude use karo

Jab annotators scores ya rankings dete hain (Likert Scale par), to relational quantities ka magnitude training me use kiya jaa sakta hai. Sabse common practice hai data ko preference direction ke along binarize karna — relative ratings ya ranking ki strength ki mixed information ko sirf chosen aur rejected completions tak reduce kar dena. Additional information (jaise preference ka magnitude) se model training improve hui hai, lekin ye standard practice nahi bani.

Ek model ne do datapoints ke beech margin m(yc, yr) use karne ka proposal diya:

Equation 5.7: L(θ) = −log(σ(rθ(yc|x) − rθ(yr|x) − m(yc, yr))). Example: har completion ko quality me 1 se 5 tak ranking di jaati hai. Agar chosen sample ko score 5 aur rejected ko 2 mila, to margin m(yc, yr) = 5 − 2 = 3. Margins compute karne ke doosre functions bhi explore kiye jaa sakte hain. Note: ek baad wale model me margin term hata diya gaya kyunki scaling ke baad diminishing improvements observe hue.

Balancing Multiple Comparisons Per Prompt

Ek study ne variable number of completions per prompt ka impact study kiya, phir bhi reward model training me unhe balance kiya. Iske liye loss updates ko per comparison per prompt weight kiya jaata hai. Implementation level par ye automatically ho jaata hai agar same prompt wale saare examples ek hi training batch me include kiye jaayein — naturally different pairs ko weight milta hai; aisa na karne se prompts par overfitting hoti thi.

Equation 5.8: L(θ) = −(1 / C(K,2)) × E(x,yc,yr)~D[ log(σ(rθ(yc|x) − rθ(yr|x))) ], jahan K ek prompt ke liye comparisons ki sankhya hai.

K-wise Loss Function — Plackett-Luce model

Kai aur formulations bhi human preferences ke suitable models bana sakti hain. Ek example, jo popular early RLHF models Starling 7B aur 34B me use hua, Plackett-Luce model par based K-wise loss function hai. Setup: prompt (state) si par K actions (a0, a1, …, aK−1) sample kiye jaate hain, phir labelers unhe rank karte hain — σi(0) sabse preferred action hota hai.

Equation 5.9 (Plackett-Luce): P(σi|si, a0, …, aK−1) = Πk=0..K−1 exp(rθ(si, aσ(k))) / Σj=k..K−1 exp(rθ(si, aσ(j))). Jab K = 2 ho, to ye Bradley-Terry (BT) model me reduce ho jaata hai. Train hone ke baad ye models RLHF training me doosre reward models ki tarah hi use hote hain.
Source: The RLHF Book, Manning, Chapter 5
← Previous5.2–5.3 Architecture aur Implementation Example (PyTorch)Next →5.5 Outcome Reward Models (ORMs)
05.5Chapter 5 — Reward Modeling

5.5 Outcome Reward Models (ORMs)

Reasoning-heavy tasks ke liye Outcome Reward Model (ORM) use kar sakte ho. ORM ka training data standard preference tuning jaisa hi banta hai — bas inductive bias alag hai: ek completion problem ka correct solution hona chahiye aur ek incorrect.

ORM kaise alag hai — per-token correctness

ORM ka model shape standard reward model jaisa hi hai — linear layer append karke ek single logit output karta hai — lekin training objective thoda alag hai: model seekhta hai ki model completion ko correct ya incorrect label kare, original language modeling objective ke saath. Architecturally, verifiers language models hote hain, ek chhote scalar head ke saath jo per-token basis par predictions output karta hai. Scalar head ek single bias parameter aur single gain parameter ke roop me implement hota hai jo language model ki final unembedding layer ke logits par operate karte hain.

Translate karein to: ye ek language modeling head hai jo per token do classes predict kar sakta hai (1 for correct, 0 for incorrect), traditional RM ke classification head ke bajay jo poori sequence ke liye ek logit output karta hai:

Equation 5.10 — ORM loss (binary cross-entropy): LCE(θ) = −E(s,r)~D[ r × log pθ(s) + (1−r) × log(1 − pθ(s)) ], jahan r ∈ {0, 1} binary label hai (1 = correct answer, 0 = incorrect), aur pθ(s) correctness ki predicted probability hai.

Implementation me per-token cross-entropy loss apply hoti hai based on completion correct hai ya nahi. Ye language modeling loss ke bahut kareeb hai — isme standard Bradley-Terry reward models jaisi structured chosen-rejected nature nahi chahiye. Code me: labels me prompt tokens ko -100 se mask kiya jaata hai, sirf completion tokens par loss compute hoti hai (F.binary_cross_entropy_with_logits(logits[mask], labels[mask].float())).

Important intuition: ORM sequence ke har token par correctness ki probability output karega. Ye noisy process ho sakta hai, kyunki updates aur loss per token propagate hote hain, outcomes aur attention mappings par depend karte hue. Ye models use me rahe hain, lekin open-source RLHF tools me kam supported hain. Ek seminal work ("Let's Verify Step by Step") me bhi yahi type ka ORM use hua tha, lekin language modeling prediction piece ke bina — final loss har token par cross-entropy thi jo predict karti thi ki final answer correct hai ya nahi. Support ki kami ki wajah se "ORM" term multiple tareekon se use hua hai.

Source: The RLHF Book, Manning, Chapter 5
← Previous5.4 Variants — margin loss, balancing, K-wise lossNext →5.6 Process Reward Models (PRMs)
05.6Chapter 5 — Reward Modeling

5.6 Process Reward Models (PRMs)

Process Reward Models (PRMs) — originally Process-supervised Reward Models — chain-of-thought reasoning process ke har step par scores output karne ke liye train kiye jaate hain. Ye standard RM se alag hain (jo sirf EOS token par score deta hai) aur ORM se bhi alag hain (jo har token par score deta hai).

PRM kaise kaam karta hai — har reasoning step par label

PRMs ko har reasoning step ke end par supervision chahiye hoti hai, phir unhe waise hi train kiya jaata hai — tokens ko unke relevant target se train kiya jaata hai: PRMs me target step hota hai, ORMs me target poori response hoti hai. Binary-labeled PRM commonly per-step cross-entropy loss se optimize hota hai:

Equation 5.11 — PRM loss: LPRM(θ) = −E(x,s)~D[ Σi=1..K ysi × log rθ(si|x) + (1 − ysi) × log(1 − rθ(si|x)) ], jahan s K annotated steps wali sampled chain-of-thought hai, ysi ∈ {0, 1} batata hai ki i-th step correct hai ya nahi, aur rθ(si|x) PRM ki predicted probability hai ki step si valid hai, original prompt x given.

Per-step label ko trainer me package karne ka example (TRL library se): separator token ki ID lo, completions me add karo, phir labels banao — [[-100] * (len(completion) - 1) + [label] for completion, label in zip(completions_ids, labels)] — matlab sirf step ke last token par label hota hai, baaki sab -100 (masked).

Traditionally PRMs ek language modeling head se train hote hain jo sirf reasoning step ke end par ek token output karta hai — jaise double newline ya koi special token par. Predictions tend karte hain: -1 incorrect, 0 neutral, 1 correct. Ye labels ye nahi batate ki model sahi raaste par hai ya nahi, bas ye ki step correct hai ya nahi.

PRM ka example construction: 3 classes wala head (nn.Linear(hidden_size, 3)), labels map hote hain -1 → 0, 0 → 1, 1 → 2 (class indices), aur loss sirf step boundaries par compute hoti hai (F.cross_entropy(logits[mask], labels[mask])). Core loss function ORM jaisi hi dikhti hai — labels alag intervals par apply hote hain.

Source: The RLHF Book, Manning, Chapter 5
← Previous5.5 Outcome Reward Models (ORMs)Next →5.7 RM vs ORM vs PRM vs Value Functions — comparison table
05.7Chapter 5 — Reward Modeling

5.7 RM vs ORM vs PRM vs Value Functions — comparison table

Alag-alag reward models ka spectrum batata hai ki RLHF aur doosri post-training methods me "quality" kitne tareekon se measure ki jaa sakti hai.

TypeOutputTrainingUse Case
Reward ModelsEOS token par chosen response ki probability se text ki qualityCompletions ke beech pairwise (ya N-wise) comparisons par contrastive lossLM features ke upar regression ya classification head
Outcome Reward ModelsHar token par answer correct hone ki probabilityLabeled outcome pairs (jaise verifiable domains par success/failure)Per-token cross-entropy wala language modeling head, har label outcome-level label hai
Process Reward ModelsReasoning steps ke end par intermediate steps ke liye reward/scoreIntermediate feedback ya stepwise annotations se train (har token reasoning step me train hota hai)Language modeling head jo sirf har reasoning step par inference chalata hai, 3 classes predict karta hai: -1, 0, 1
Value FunctionsCurrent state given expected returnSequence ke har point par regression se trainHar token par output wali classification

Kuch notes — table me bahut edge cases hain: preference tuning aur reasoning training dono me value functions ka discount factor aksar 1 hota hai, jo value function ko ORM ke aur kareeb le aata hai, lekin training loss alag hoti hai. PRM ko intermediate state se rollouts karke aur outcome data collect karke supervise kiya jaa sakta hai — ye multiple ideas ko blend karta hai, lekin agar loss per reasoning step labels par hai, to use PRM hi kehna best hai.

Source: The RLHF Book, Manning, Chapter 5
← Previous5.6 Process Reward Models (PRMs)Next →5.8 Generative Reward Modeling — LLM-as-a-judge
05.8Chapter 5 — Reward Modeling

5.8 Generative Reward Modeling — LLM-as-a-judge

Preference data ki cost ki wajah se ek bada research area emerge hua: existing language models ko human preferences ka judge bana kar use karna — evaluation settings me bhi.

Judge prompt — MT-Bench wala example

Core idea: language model ko instructions ke saath prompt karo ki judge kaise karna hai, phir prompt aur do completions do (bilkul waisa hi jaise human labelers ko diya jaata hai). Seminal MT-Bench work ka example prompt: system kehta hai "Please act as an impartial judge and evaluate the quality of the responses provided by two AI assistants" — helpfulness, relevance, accuracy, depth, creativity aur detail ke level ko consider karna; pehle dono responses compare karke short explanation dena; position biases avoid karna (order ka verdict par influence na ho); length ko evaluation influence na karne dena; assistants ke certain names ko favor na karna; jitna objective ho sake utna rehna; phir final verdict strictly is format me dena: "[[A]]" agar assistant A behtar hai, "[[B]]" agar B behtar hai, aur "[[C]]" tie ke liye.

LLM-as-a-judge evaluation ke liye effective nikla — isse AlpacaEval, Arena-Hard aur WildBench jaise kai evaluations spawn hue — aur kai logon ne reward models ki jagah LLM-as-a-judge se preference data create aur use karna shuru kar diya.

Is par ek poora field emerge hua — "Generative Reward Models" (kuch models specifically effective judges banne ke liye train kiye gaye) — lekin RM evaluations par ye existing reward models se peeche rehte hain, jo dikhata hai ki reward modeling current RLHF ke liye ek important technique hai. LLM-as-a-judge workflows ki robustness improve karne ki ek common trick hai sampling temperature 0 use karna taaki ratings ki variance kam ho.

Source: The RLHF Book, Manning, Chapter 5
← Previous5.7 RM vs ORM vs PRM vs Value Functions — comparison tableNext →5.9 Further Reading — RM benchmarks ki duniya
05.9Chapter 5 — Reward Modeling

5.9 Further Reading — RM benchmarks ki duniya

Reward modeling ke liye academic literature 2024 me establish hui. Early progress ka bulk benchmarks establish karne aur behavior modes identify karne me raha.

Pehla RM benchmark, RewardBench, reward models test karne ke liye common infrastructure deta tha. Uske baad se RM evaluation general post-trained models wali evaluations jaisi expand ho gayi — kuch evaluations domains par prediction accuracy test karti hain jahan true answers known hain, ya "vibes" jaisi jo LLM-as-a-judge ya doosre benchmarks se correlation se ki jaati hain.

Benchmarks — categories ke hisaab se

  • Text-only (general chat / preferences): RMB, RewardBench2, Preference Proxy Evaluations, RM-Bench
  • Specialized text-only (math, etc.): multilingual reward bench (M-RewardBench), RAG-RewardBench (retrieval augmented generation), ReWordBench (typos), RewardMATH, AceMath-RewardBench
  • Process RMs: PRM Bench, ProcessBench, aur visual benchmarks VisualProcessBench, ViLBench
  • Agentic RMs: Agent-RewardBench, CUARewardBench
  • Multimodal: MJ-Bench, Multimodal RewardBench, VL RewardBench, VLRMBench

Reward models train karne ki progress samajhne ke liye naye training methods dekh sakte ho — aspect-conditioned models, high-quality human datasets, scaling experiments, extensive experimentation, ya debiasing data.

Chapter 5 ka takeaway: Bradley-Terry loss (Eq 5.5/5.6) standard hai — chosen vs rejected par sigmoid. ORM correctness ko per-token classify karta hai, PRM reasoning steps ko per-step score karta hai, aur generative reward models (LLM-as-a-judge) evaluation me useful hain lekin RM benchmarks par peeche rehte hain. Reward model train karte waqt sirf 1 epoch — overfitting se bachna.
Source: The RLHF Book, Manning, Chapter 5

06.1Chapter 6 — Reinforcement Learning

Chapter 6 intro — Reinforcement Learning: policy ko reward se update karo

RLHF process me reinforcement learning algorithm model ke weights ko reward model ke feedback ke hisaab se dheere-dheere update karta hai. Policy — train ho raha model — training set ke prompts par completions generate karta hai, phir reward model unhe score karta hai, aur phir RL optimizer is information ke basis par gradient steps leta hai.

Ye algorithms kai epochs tak chalaye jaate hain — aksar thousands ya millions of batches, prompts ke bade set par, beech-beech me gradient updates ke saath. RLHF ko popular banane wale algorithms policy-gradient RL algorithms the — jaise Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO), Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO), aur REINFORCE. Ye recently generated samples se apna model update karte hain (na ki replay buffer me scores store karke, jaise Deep Q-Networks (DQN) karte the).

Machine learning level par ye section RLHF process ka sabse complex subject hai. Haan, jaise most modern AI models me hota hai, success ka sabse bada determining factor inputs ke roop me diya gaya data hota hai.

ChatGPT ke aane par ye largely known tha ki unhone PPO ka ek variant use kiya tha, aur kai initial efforts usi par bane. Samay ke saath multiple research projects ne REINFORCE-style algorithms ka promise dikhaya — PPO se simpler hone ke liye tout kiye gaye, bina reward model ke (memory bachti hai, isiliye kam GPUs chahiye) aur simpler value estimation ke saath (koi Generalized Advantage Estimation, GAE, nahi — jo policy gradient algorithms me variance reduction ke liye advantages compute karne ka method hai). Aur algorithms emerge hue, jinme GRPO khaas taur par reasoning tasks me popular hai — lekin general me kai algorithms ko specific task ke liye tune kiya jaa sakta hai.

Is chapter me (s, a) notation RL literature se use hoti hai, jahan s states aur a actions denote karte hain. Language model context me aksar (x, y) dikhega, jahan x prompt hai aur y completion. (s, a) framing zyada general hai — ye algorithms sequential decision problems ke liye design kiye gaye the jahan har timestep par actions liye jaate hain. Lekin kai RLHF implementations poori completion ko ek single action treat karte hain, jisse (x, y) notation equally valid ho jaati hai.

Source: The RLHF Book, Manning, Chapter 6
← Previous5.9 Further Reading — RM benchmarks ki duniyaNext →6.1 Policy Gradient Algorithms — return, value, gradient
06.2Chapter 6 — Reinforcement Learning

6.1 Policy Gradient Algorithms — return, value, gradient

Policy gradient algorithms ka goal hai expected return maximize karna — discounted future rewards ka sum. Is section me woh derivation hai jo PPO, GRPO aur REINFORCE sab ki neev hai.

Return aur value function

Agent ka objective, jise return kehte hain, time t par discounted future rewards ka sum hai (γ ∈ [0, 1] woh factor hai jo near-term rewards ko prioritize karta hai):

Equation 6.1: Gt = Rt+1 + γRt+2 + … = Σk=0..∞ γk Rt+k+1
Equation 6.2: Gt = γGt+1 + Rt+1 (recursive form)
Equation 6.3: V(s) = E[Gt | St = s] — value function, current state given estimated future return.

Saare policy gradient algorithms ek policy πθ(a|s) optimize karte hain taaki expected return maximize ho. Objective ko induced value function se express kiya jaa sakta hai:

Equation 6.4: J(θ) = Σs dπθ(s) × Vπθ(s), jahan dπθ(s) policy πθ se induced state-visitation distribution hai. Finite MDP me ye saare states par sum hai, lekin practice me hum ise exactly compute kabhi nahi karte — current policy se rollouts sample karke estimate karte hain. RLHF me rollouts train ho rahe model se generations ke complete sequences hote hain: prompts xi dataset se sample karo, completions yi ~ πθ(·|xi) generate karo, phir empirical average lo: Ĵ(θ) = (1/B) Σi=1..B R(xi, yi).

Policy gradient — log-derivative trick

Policy gradient algorithms ka core hai finite-time expected return par gradient compute karna. Parameter update: θ ← θ + α∇θJ(θ), jahan α learning rate hai (Eq 6.5). Objective ko trajectory expectation ke roop me likha jaa sakta hai: J(θ) = Eτ~πθ[R(τ)] (Eq 6.6), jahan τ = (s0, a0, s1, a1, …) ek trajectory hai aur R(τ) uska total reward hai. Ise integral ke roop me bhi likha jaa sakta hai: J(θ) = ∫ pθ(τ)R(τ)dτ (Eq 6.7).

Trajectory probability: pθ(τ) = p(s0) × Πt=0..∞ πθ(at|st) × p(st+1|st, at) (Eq 6.8). Gradient lene par (Eq 6.9-6.11) log-derivative trick use hoti hai: ∇θ log pθ(τ) = ∇θpθ(τ) / pθ(τ), isiliye ∇θJ(θ) = Eτ~πθ[∇θ log pθ(τ) × R(τ)].

Log probability expand karne par: log pθ(τ) = log p(s0) + Σ log πθ(at|st) + Σ log p(st+1|st, at). Gradient lene par pehle aur teesre terms zero ho jaate hain (initial state aur environment dynamics θ par depend nahi karte) — sirf ∇θ log πθ(at|st) bachta hai. Isiliye: ∇θ log pθ(τ) = Σt=0..∞ ∇θ log πθ(at|st).

General form — Ψ (psi) taxonomy

Equation 6.12: g = ∇θJ(θ) = Eτ~πθ[ Σt=0..∞ ∇θ log πθ(at|st) × Ψt ], jahan Ψt ye ho sakta hai: (1) R(τ) — trajectory ka total reward; (2) Σt'=t..∞ rt' — action at ke baad ka reward (return G); (3) Σ rt' − b(st) — baselined version; (4) Qπ(st, at) — state-action value function; (5) Aπ(st, at) — advantage function (sabse kam theoretical variance, agar accurately compute ho); (6) rt + Vπ(st+1) − Vπ(st) — Temporal Difference (TD) residual.

Language models ke liye: agar s + a ko prompt s ka continuation a mana jaaye, to Q(s, a) = V(s + a), jo ek alag advantage trick deta hai:

Equation 6.13: A(s, a) = Q(s, a) − V(s) = V(s + a) − V(s) = r + γV(s + a) − V(s) — reward, prompt ki value, aur poori utterance ki discounted value ka combination.

Vanilla policy gradient — variance problem

Equation 6.14: ∇θJ(θ) = Eτ[ Σt=0..T ∇θ log πθ(at|st) × Rt ]
Equation 6.15 (advantage form): ∇θJ(θ) = Eτ[ Σt=0..T ∇θ log πθ(at|st) × Aπθ(st, at) ]

Vanilla policy gradient ki common problem hai gradient updates me high variance — return G ka estimate aksar chhote rollout sets se hota hai jo noise ke prati susceptible hote hain (jaise temperature > 0 par language models se generation ki stochastic nature). Sparse rewards wale domains me variance zyada hoti hai, kyunki zyada samples 0 ya 1 hote hain, closely clustered nahi. Ise mitigate karne ke liye baselines use hote hain — state ki value ke relative downstream action ko normalize karna (jaise Advantage, Q value aur value ka difference). Simplest baselines batch rewards ka average ya moving average hote hain. Baselines gradients ko de-bias bhi kar sakte hain — Ea~π(a|s)[∇θ log πθ(a|s)] = 0 — learning signal substantially improve ho jaata hai.

Source: The RLHF Book, Manning, Chapter 6
← PreviousChapter 6 intro — Reinforcement Learning: policy ko reward se update karoNext →6.1.2–6.1.4 REINFORCE, RLOO aur PPO
06.3Chapter 6 — Reinforcement Learning

6.1.2–6.1.4 REINFORCE, RLOO aur PPO

Teen foundational algorithms — REINFORCE (simplest), RLOO (leave-one-out baseline), aur PPO (clipped surrogate) — ek hi policy gradient neev par bane hain, bas variance aur stability handle karne ka tareeka alag hai.

REINFORCE — naam ka matlab

REINFORCE likely ek backronym hai, lekin uske components modern RL algorithms ke liye relevant hain. Seminal paper ke hisaab se naam ka matlab hai: "REward Increment = Nonnegative Factor X Offset Reinforcement X Characteristic Eligibility." Teen pieces: (1) Nonnegative factor: learning rate (step size), jo positive number hona chahiye, jaise α; (2) Offset Reinforcement: baseline b ya reward ko normalize karne wala doosra factor, stability improve karne ke liye; (3) Characteristic Eligibility: learning kaise per token attribute hoti hai — aksar modern equations me policy ki log probabilities.

Equation 6.16: Δθ = α(r − b)e
Equation 6.17 (modern form): ∇θJ(θ) = Eτ~πθ[ Σt=0..T ∇θ log πθ(at|st) × (Gt − b(st)) ]
Equation 6.18 (advantage form): ∇θJ(θ) = Eτ~πθ[ Σt=0..T ∇θ log πθ(at|st) × At ]
REINFORCE vanilla policy gradient ka ek specific implementation hai jo gradient ka Monte Carlo estimator use karta hai.

RLOO — leave-one-out baseline

REINFORCE Leave One Out (RLOO) ka core difference ye hai ki baseline compute karne ke liye batch ke doosre samples ka average reward liya jaata hai — saare rewards ka average lene ke bajay. Ye tabhi kaam karta hai jab ek state (prompt) par multiple trajectories (completions) generate ki jaayein — jo language models ko RL se fine-tune karne ke kai domains me common practice hai.

Equation 6.19: b(s, ak) = (1/(K−1)) × Σi=1..K, i≠k R(s, ai), jahan K ek prompt par sampled trajectories ki sankhya hai.
Equation 6.20: A(s, ak) = R(s, ak) − b(s, ak)
Equation 6.21 (equivalent form): A(s, ak) = (K/(K−1)) × (R(s, ak) − (1/K) × Σi=1..K R(s, ai))

Ye ek simple, low-variance per-prompt advantage estimate hai jo GRPO ke group-relative advantage se closely related hai. Practically, GRPO-style training mainly isme differ karta hai ki KL regularizer kaise apply hota hai (explicit loss term vs reward me fold karna) aur PPO-style ratio clipping use hoti hai ya nahi. Canonical GRPO KL penalty ko loss level par apply karta hai, jabki RLOO ya traditional policy-gradients ki derivation KL penalty ko reward me apply karti hai. RLHF se reasoning aur RLVR ki taraf transition ke saath KL penalties ki prevalence overall kam hui hai — kai reasoning adaptations ne unhe poori tarah off kar diya hai. RLOO ka advantage PPO ki clipping ke saath bhi combine kiya jaa sakta hai — ye dikhata hai ki ye algorithms kitne similar hain.

Ek aur key difference: value network use na karne wale algorithms (RLOO jaise) loss compute karte waqt har token ko wahi sequence-level advantage (ya reward) assign karte hain. PPO jaise learned value network wale algorithms har token ko alag value assign karte hain, EOS token par mile final reward se discount karte hue. KL distance penalty ke saath, RLOO completion par per-token KL aggregate karke us scalar ko sequence reward me fold karta hai, isiliye resulting advantage saare tokens par broadcast hota hai. PPO At compute karne se pehle per-token reward se per-token KL subtract karta hai — token-level credit assignment. GRPO typically sequence-level advantage retain karta hai lekin loss me ek alag per-token term add karta hai, reward se subtract karne ke bajay.

PPO — clipped surrogate objective

Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO) Deep RL ki successes ke peeche foundational algorithms me se ek hai (jaise DOTA 2 master karne wala project). PPO jo objective maximize karta hai:

Equation 6.22: J(θ) = min( (πθ(a|s)/πθold(a|s)) × A, clip(πθ(a|s)/πθold(a|s), 1−ε, 1+ε) × A )
Yahan πθ(a|s) current policy hai aur πθold(a|s) woh policy hai jisse training data collect kiya gaya tha (previous iteration wali policy). In dono ke beech ka ratio importance sampling se aata hai — jo old policy ke under collect kiye gaye data ko reuse karke nayi policy ke gradients estimate karne deta hai.

Bina constraints ke, is importance-weighted objective ko optimize karne se destructively large policy updates ho sakte hain jab ratio 1 se bahut door chala jaaye. PPO ratio ko [1−ε, 1+ε] range me clip karke ye solve karta hai — policy ek hi update me zyada drastically change nahi kar sakti.

Equation 6.23 (clipped surrogate): J(θ) = Et[ min(rt(θ)At, clip(rt(θ), 1−ε, 1+ε)At) ], jahan rt(θ) = πθ(at|st) / πθold(at|st)
Equation 6.24 (per-token version, language models ke liye): J(θ) = (1/|a|) × Σt=0..|a| min( (πθ/πθold) × At, clip(πθ/πθold, 1−ε, 1+ε) × At ). 1/|a| se average karna common implementation practice se aata hai, formal derivation se nahi.

Policy ratio R(θ) = πθ(a|s) / πθold(a|s) (Eq 6.25) PPO aur related algorithms ka centerpiece hai. Kisi bhi batch ke liye policy ratio pehle gradient step par 1 se shuru hota hai (kyunki πθ aur πθold same hain). Agle gradient step me ratio 1 se upar hoga agar gradient step ne positive advantage wale tokens ki likelihood badha di, ya 1 se neeche doosre case me. Common practice hai per batch 1–4 gradient steps lena, phir πθold update karna.

PPO objective samjho — positive aur negative advantage

PPO objective ko objective vs policy ratio ke plot ki do lines se visualize kiya jaa sakta hai. Objective dono cases ko cleverly min operation se control karta hai — update ko policy ratio 1 se zyada se zyada epsilon distance tak push kiya jaata hai. Trust region ke andar PPO doosre policy gradient algorithms jaisa hi operate karta hai — ye by design hai. Trust region ka concept numerical optimization literature se aaya hai, lekin Deep RL me Trust Region Policy Optimization (TRPO) se popular hua — jo PPO ka predecessor mana jaata hai. Trust region woh area hai jahan full policy-gradient steps apply hote hain, kyunki updates PPO objective ke max/min operations se "clip" nahi hote.

  • Positive advantage (A > 0): action beneficial tha, iski likelihood badhani hai. Gradient steps sirf tab hote hain jab πnew(a) ≤ (1+ε)πold(a). Jab πnew(a) > (1+ε)πold(a) ho jaaye, to koi update nahi hota — clipped objective ka gradient 0 ho jaata hai. Intuition: action pehle se hi nayi policy me zyada expressed hai, use over-reinforce nahi karna.
  • Negative advantage (A < 0): action detrimental tha, iski likelihood kam karni hai. Gradient steps sirf tab hote hain jab πnew(a) ≥ (1−ε)πold(a). Jab πnew(a) < (1−ε)πold(a) ho jaaye, to koi update nahi — action pehle se hi kam likely hai, use over-suppress nahi karna.

Yaad rakhna crucial hai: trust region ke andar PPO roughly standard policy gradient jaisa hi hai.

Value functions aur PPO

PPO ke andar value function model ki ek additional copy hoti hai jo har token ka value predict karti hai — traditional RL me kisi moment se future return predict karna, aksar discounting ke saath. Ye value PPO me learned baseline ke roop me use hoti hai — REINFORCE wale simple Monte Carlo version ka evolution (jise learned value network nahi chahiye). Ye highlight karta hai ki PPO REINFORCE aur vanilla policy-gradient ka evolution hai — optimization form aur baseline dono me. Practically, language models ke liye PPO me ye har token ke baad ke return ko predict karta hai, KL penalties deduct karne ke baad.

Value functions seekhne ke kuch methods (targets) hain. Generalized Advantage Estimation (GAE) state-of-the-art aur canonical implementation mana jaata hai modern systems me, lekin ye zyada complex hai kyunki ye multiple steps par value prediction error compute karta hai. Value function ko rollouts se Monte Carlo estimates se bhi seekha jaa sakta hai. PPO ke do losses hote hain — ek value function seekhne ke liye aur ek us value function se policy update karne ke liye. Book ek simple value network loss ka code deti hai: Monte Carlo returns per token (terminals par reset), PPO-style value clipping (εv jaise 0.2), response tokens par mask karke aggregate karna, aur advantages = targets − v_pred (GAE ke bina).

Source: The RLHF Book, Manning, Chapter 6
