07.4Chapter 7 — Reasoning & Inference-Time Scaling

Looking ahead — reasoning training ka future

Reasoning models ka landscape AI research ke kisi bhi area se tez evolve ho raha hai. Jab tak ye chapter publish hoga, Table 7.1 incomplete hogi aur kuch common practices naye techniques se superseded ho chuki hongi. Phir bhi kuch cheezein clear hain.

Systematic understanding ki koshish

OLMo 3 Think reasoning model ke full training lifecycle ka sabse comprehensive open documentation hai — har stage par checkpoints aur data, research community ke liye — aur lagbhag 4 hafte ki training run 220 GPUs par. RL scaling properties ko formalize karne ka kaam bhi shuru ho gaya hai — compute, data aur performance ke beech relationships jo pehle sirf practitioners ki intuition thi.

Distillation aur inference calls

Core RL-trained models ke alawa aur methods explore ho rahe hain: bade RL-trained model se chhote model me reasoning behavior distill karna (instruction tuning se), zyada inference calls compose karna, aur bhi. Important correlation ye hai: downstream performance aur generate kiye gaye tokens ki sankhya ke beech — warna woh sirf wasted energy hai.

Bottom line

Reinforcement learning cake metaphor ki "cherry on top" se graduate karke frontier model training ka load-bearing component ban gaya hai. Difficulty filtering, format rewards jaise minor techniques final answers nahi hain, lekin ye field ki current best understanding hain ki models se reasoning kaise elicit ki jaaye. Agli generation ke methods alag dikhenge, lekin woh in foundations par banenge.

Source: The RLHF Book, Manning, Chapter 7
← PreviousReasoning training methods — STaR se lekar Table 7.1 takNext →Direct Alignment Algorithms — DPO kya hai aur kaise kaam karta hai
08.1Chapter 8 — Direct Alignment Algorithms

Direct Alignment Algorithms — DPO kya hai aur kaise kaam karta hai

Direct Alignment Algorithms (DAAs) wohi RLHF objective solve karte hain — lekin bina intermediate reward model train kiye aur bina reinforcement learning optimizers ke. Matlab: wahi preference data, wahi objective, lekin implementation bahut simple, compute kam, experimentation aasan. Sabse prominent DAA hai DPO — Direct Preference Optimization (May 2023).

Wohi objective, Eq 8.1

Eq 8.1 — RLHF objective: maxπ Ex∼D Ey∼π(y|x) [rθ(x, y)] − β DKL(π(y|x) ∥ πref(y|x))
Matlab: expected reward maximize karo, minus β times KL distance from reference model.

DPO ke release ke baad, community ko sahi data aur hyperparameters samajhne me thoda time laga — khaas taur par surprisingly low learning rates. Phir bahut se popular models ne DPO ya uske variants use kiye: Zephyr-β (Oct 2023, jisne isko kickstart kiya), Llama 3 Instruct, Tülu 2 aur 3, Nemotron 4 340B, aur bhi. Technically pehla modern DAA SLiC-HF tha, lekin woh catch on nahi hua.

Notation

Is chapter me x = prompt aur y = completion hai. Methods full prompt-completion pairs par operate karte hain, individual tokens par nahi.

DPO loss — Eq 8.2

Eq 8.2 — DPO loss: LDPO(πθ; πref) = −E(x, yc, yr)∼D [log σ(β log (πθ(yc|x) / πref(yc|x)) − β log (πθ(yr|x) / πref(yr|x)))]
yc = chosen response, yr = rejected response, σ = sigmoid.

β ek hyperparameter hai jo reward optimization aur KL distance ke beech balance karta hai — over-optimization ko control karne ke liye crucial. Loss tab kam hota hai jab chosen response ka log-ratio rejected response ke log-ratio se bada ho (reference model se normalized). Practice me ye model ke sequence ke tokens ke log-probabilities ka sum hai. DPO chosen aur rejected responses ke beech probabilities ka delta badha raha hai.

Implicit reward — Eq 8.3

Eq 8.3 — implicit reward: r(x, y) = β log (πr(y|x) / πref(y|x))
Yahan πr woh exact optimal reward policy hai jise solve kiya ja raha hai.

Ye Bradley-Terry reward ko optimal policy ke respect me derive karne se aata hai (Eq 8.17). Implicit reward model dikhata hai: "human preference data ki probability, optimal policy ke terms me, reward model ke terms me nahi."

DPO gradient — Eq 8.4

Eq 8.4 — DPO gradient: ∇θLDPO = −β E [σ(rθ(x, yr) − rθ(x, yc)) (∇θ log π(yc|x) − ∇θ log π(yr|x))]
  • Sigmoid wala term (0 se 1): weight tab bada hota hai jab reward estimate galat ho — jab rejected sample chosen se zyada preferred ho, update bada hona chahiye.
  • Bracket wala term: chosen response yc ki likelihood badhao, rejected yr ki likelihood ghatao.
  • β: completions ko sahi order karne aur KL distance ke beech balance control karta hai.

Core intuition — "Your Language Model is Secretly a Reward Model"

DPO ek implicit reward model fit kar raha hai jiska corresponding optimal policy closed form me extract ki jaa sakti hai (gradient descent aur ML tools ki wajah se). Closed form ka matlab: exact gradient straightforward implement karna, reward model train karke aur completions sample karke us tak proxy se pahunchne ki zaroorat nahi. Aksar galat samjha jaata hai ki DPO seedha policy train karta hai — asal me DPO core me ek reward model seekh raha hai, isi liye paper ka subtitle hai "Your Language Model is Secretly a Reward Model". Derivations padhna poori understanding ke liye zaroori hai.

DPO diye gaye data aur specific KL constraint β ke liye RLHF objective ka exact solution deta hai — kyunki generations online nahi hain jaise policy gradient algorithms me. Isi liye DPO me β tune karna online RL methods ke mukable aasan hota hai, lekin crucially optimal value model aur data par depend karta hai. Har batch me, DPO seedha optimal solution ki taraf gradient steps leta hai. Ye policy gradient methods se bahut simple hai.

Source: The RLHF Book, Manning, Chapter 8
← PreviousLooking ahead — reasoning training ka futureNext →DPO derivation, Part 1 — optimal RLHF solution
08.2Chapter 8 — Direct Alignment Algorithms

DPO derivation, Part 1 — optimal RLHF solution

DPO derivation ke do primary parts hain: pehla, woh policy ka form jo RLHF objective ko optimally solve karta hai; doosra, pairwise preference data (Bradley-Terry model) se us solution tak pahunchna. Ye section Part 1 hai — Eq 8.5 se 8.17 tak.

Step 1 — objective phir se (Eq 8.5)

Objective wahi hai: maxπ Ex∼D Ey∼π(y|x) [r(x, y)] − β DKL(π(y|x) ∥ πref(y|x)). Dual expectation sirf expected reward compute karne wali sampling par apply hoti hai; KL term analytical expression hai.

Step 2 — KL expand karo (Eq 8.6, 8.7)

KL-divergence ki definition: DKL(π ∥ πref) = Ey∼π[log (π(y|x) / πref(y|x))]. Dono terms ab same expectation share karte hain (y ∼ π(y|x)), to combine karo:

Eq 8.6: maxπ Ex∼D Ey∼π(y|x) [r(x, y) − β log (π(y|x) / πref(y|x))]
Eq 8.7: = maxπ (Ex∼D Ey∼π(y|x)[r(x, y)] − β Ex∼D Ey∼π(y|x)[log (π(y|x) / πref(y|x))])

Step 3 — min me badlo, β se divide karo (Eq 8.8, 8.9)

Eq 8.8: = minπ (−E[r(x, y)] + β E[log (π(y|x) / πref(y|x))])
Eq 8.9: = minπ (Ex∼D Ey∼π(y|x) [log (π(y|x) / πref(y|x)) − (1/β) r(x, y)])

Step 4 — partition function Z(x) (Eq 8.10, 8.11)

Eq 8.10: Z(x) = Σy πref(y|x) exp((1/β) r(x, y))
Partition function reference policy par normalization factor hai — saare possible responses y par sum.

Eq 8.11 me ye substitute hota hai: min Ex∼D Ey∼π(y|x) [log (π(y|x) / ((1/Z(x)) πref(y|x) exp((1/β) r(x, y)))) − log Z(x)].

Step 5 — log Z(x) add/subtract karke regroup karo (Eq 8.12–8.15)

Bracket ke andar wale part (Eq 8.12: log (π(y|x)/πref(y|x)) − (1/β) r(x, y)) me log Z(x) − log Z(x) add karo (Eq 8.13), terms group karo (Eq 8.14), phir log(x) + log(y) = log(x·y) use karke aur (1/β) r(x, y) ko log exp((1/β) r(x, y)) likh kar Eq 8.11 pao (Eq 8.15).

Step 6 — KL distance ke roop me dekho (Eq 8.16, 8.17)

Eq 8.16: minπ Ex∼D [DKL(π(y|x) ∥ (1/Z(x)) πref(y|x) exp((1/β) r(x, y))) − log Z(x)]
Z(x) final answer par depend nahi karta, to ignore karo. Gibb's inequality kehti hai ye tab minimize hota hai jab distance 0 ho — matlab dono quantities equal hon! Isi se optimal policy milti hai:
Eq 8.17 — optimal policy: π*(y|x) = (1/Z(x)) πref(y|x) exp((1/β) r(x, y))
Source: The RLHF Book, Manning, Chapter 8
← PreviousDirect Alignment Algorithms — DPO kya hai aur kaise kaam karta haiNext →DPO derivation, Part 2 — Bradley-Terry se DPO loss tak
08.3Chapter 8 — Direct Alignment Algorithms

DPO derivation, Part 2 — Bradley-Terry se DPO loss tak

Part 1 me optimal policy π* mil gayi. Part 2 me use Bradley-Terry preference model me substitute karke DPO loss tak pahuncha jaata hai (Eq 8.18–8.26), phir gradient derive kiya jaata hai (Eq 8.27–8.29).

Bradley-Terry model (Eq 8.18)

Eq 8.18: p*(y1 ≻ y2 | x) = exp(r*(x, y1)) / (exp(r*(x, y1)) + exp(r*(x, y2)))

Optimal reward ke liye solve karo (Eq 8.19–8.22)

Eq 8.17 ka dono taraf logarithm lo (Eq 8.19), log(abc) = log a + log b + log c se expand karo (Eq 8.20: log π*(y|x) = −log Z(x) + log πref(y|x) + (1/β) r*(x, y)), phir r*(x, y) ke liye rearrange karo (Eq 8.21: (1/β) r*(x, y) = log π*(y|x) − log πref(y|x) + log Z(x)), dono taraf β se multiply karo:

Eq 8.22: r*(x, y) = β log (π*(y|x) / πref(y|x)) + β log Z(x)

Bradley-Terry me substitute karo (Eq 8.23–8.26)

Reward ko Eq 8.18 me substitute karo (Eq 8.23). Exponential expressions ko ea+b = eaeb me decompose karke elog(Z(x)) terms cancel karo (Eq 8.24). Phir numerator aur denominator ko exp(−β log (π*(y1|x)/πref(y1|x))) se multiply karo (Eq 8.25), aur sigmoid ki definition σ(x) = 1 / (1 + e−x) use karo:

Eq 8.26: p*(y1 ≻ y2 | x) = σ(β log (π*(y1|x) / πref(y1|x)) − β log (π*(y2|x) / πref(y2|x)))
Ye hi DPO loss function hai, jaise Eq 8.2 me dikhaya gaya. DPO paper me Plackett-Luce model ke liye bhi derivation hai, jo practice me bahut kam use hoti hai.

Gradient derivation (Eq 8.27–8.29)

Eq 8.26 ka gradient model parameters ke respect me lo (Eq 8.27). Identities use karo: sigmoid ka derivative σ'(x) = σ(x)(1 − σ(x)), log ka derivative d/dx log x = 1/x, aur σ(−x) = 1 − σ(x). u = β log(πθ(yc|x)/πref(yc|x)) − β log(πθ(yr|x)/πref(yr|x)) set karo (Eq 8.28: ∇θLDPO = −E[(σ'(u)/σ(u)) ∇θu]), expand karo to Eq 8.4 wala gradient milta hai (Eq 8.29).

Source: The RLHF Book, Manning, Chapter 8
← PreviousDPO derivation, Part 1 — optimal RLHF solutionNext →DPO ki weaknesses aur variants — preference displacement
08.4Chapter 8 — Direct Alignment Algorithms

DPO ki weaknesses aur variants — preference displacement

DPO simple hai, lekin uski weaknesses par bahut se variants propose hue hain. Core issue: DPO har preference pair ko equal weight deta hai, jabki asal me kuch pairs me richer label hota hai. Aur ek numerical issue hai — preference displacement.

Variants jo har pair ko equal treat nahi karte

  • REBEL (REgression to RElative REward Based RL): reward model se signal add karta hai — chosen aur rejected responses ke beech margin — sirf pairwise preference data ki jagah, taaki RLHF problem zyada accurately solve ho.
  • cDPO (Conservative DPO) aur IPO (Identity Preference Optimization): preference data me noise assume karke overfitting address karte hain. cDPO assume karta hai N percent data galat labelled hai; IPO optimization ko soften karta hai — preference probability ko nonlinear function banata hai, Bradley-Terry assumption se hat kar, Ψ(q) = log(q / (1−q)).
  • ODPO (DPO with an offset): preferred aur dispreferred response ki likelihood ka difference ek offset value se zyada hona chahiye — har pair ko equal treat mat karo, lekin iski cost hai zyada difficult labeling environment.

Loss ya efficiency badalne wale variants

  • ORPO (Odds Ratio Policy Optimization): policy model ko seedha update karta hai — chosen response ki taraf pull (IFT loss jaisa) plus chosen par chhota penalty. Reference model ki zaroorat khatm — setup simple. Best view: DPO-inspired, DPO derivative nahi.
  • SimPO (Simple Preference Optimization): log-probabilities ko sum karne ki jagah average karta hai (length normalization add karke) performance improve karne ke liye.

Preference displacement — Fig 8.2

DPO optimization sirf chosen aur rejected responses ki probability ke beech margin badhane ke liye drive karta hai. Numerically, model dono — chosen aur rejected — ki probabilities ghata deta hai, lekin rejected zyada extent tak ghatti hai (Fig 8.2). Intuitively ye clear nahi hai ki ye kaise generalize karta hai, lekin kaam ne posit kiya hai ki ye unaddressed behaviors ki probability badhata hai — matlab woh tokens jo language model generate kar sakta hai, lekin post-training datasets ki distribution me nahi hain. Simple methods — jaise Cal-DPO (optimization process adjust karta hai) aur AlphaPO (reward shape modify karta hai) — is displacement ko mitigate karte hain. Practice me iska exact impact achhi tarah nahi pata, lekin ye ek potential reason hai ki online methods vanilla DPO se outperform kar sakte hain.

Online variants

DPO-like methods ka performance ceiling online (RL-based) RLHF methods se kam hone ka sabse bada reason: training signal previous ya doosre models ke completions se aata hai. Online variants ye limitation alleviate karte hain — current model se generations sample karke aur training time par preference signal incorporate karke. Online DPO current model se generations sample karta hai, D2PO (Discriminator-Guided DPO) reward model relabelling se on-the-fly naya preference data banata hai, aur bhi variants hain.

Aur bhi lambi list hai — Direct Nash Optimization (DNO), Binary Classifier Optimization (BCO) — lekin book ka point: algorithm ka choice initial model aur data se bahut kam important hai.

Source: The RLHF Book, Manning, Chapter 8
← PreviousDPO derivation, Part 2 — Bradley-Terry se DPO loss takNext →DPO implementation — code aur considerations
08.5Chapter 8 — Direct Alignment Algorithms

DPO implementation — code aur considerations

DAAs jaise DPO policy gradient optimizers se bahut alag implement hote hain. DPO loss, original implementation se, kuch lines me summarize ho jaata hai — aur ye standard language model training stacks me use ho sakta hai, kyunki ye information model ke forward pass me pehle se collate hoti hai (plus ek reference model).

DPO loss code

pi_logratios = policy_chosen_logps - policy_rejected_logps
ref_logratios = reference_chosen_logps - reference_rejected_logps

logits = pi_logratios - ref_logratios   # also known as h_{pi_theta}^{y_w,y_l}

losses = -F.logsigmoid(beta * logits)

chosen_rewards = beta * (policy_chosen_logps - reference_chosen_logps).detach()
rejected_rewards = beta * (policy_rejected_logps - reference_rejected_logps).detach()

Do considerations

  • 1. KL distance static hai: DPO aur doosre algorithms me KL distance β parameter se explicitly set hoti hai — jo distance penalty aur optimization ke beech balance karta hai. Aisa is liye kyunki DPO data ke diye gaye RLHF objective ke optimal solution ki taraf gradient steps leta hai — β term se set solution par exactly step karta hai. Dusri taraf, RL-based optimizers batch aur recent data ke basis par steps lete hain.
  • 2. Log-probabilities caching: Simple DPO implementations policy aur reference models ke forward passes ek saath karte hain (loss function ki convenience ke liye) — lekin isse memory double ho jaati hai aur GPU usage badhta hai. Isse bachne ke liye, reference model ki log-probabilities pehle training dataset par compute karo, phir loss compute karte aur parameters update karte time use refer karo — peak memory usage 50% kam ho jaata hai.
Source: The RLHF Book, Manning, Chapter 8
← PreviousDPO ki weaknesses aur variants — preference displacementNext →Synthetic preference data aur DAA vs RL — kaunsa kab
08.6Chapter 8 — Direct Alignment Algorithms

Synthetic preference data aur DAA vs RL — kaunsa kab

Aaj ke popular preference fine-tuning datasets zyada tar synthetic preferences hain — ek frontier model doosre models ke outputs ko winner ya loser rate karta hai. Aur sawal ye hai: kya RL ke inner workings (value functions, policy gradients) ki zaroorat hai, ya DAA kaafi hai?

Synthetic preference datasets

Prominent examples: UltraFeedback (is category ka pehla), Tülu 3 (expanded UltraFeedback methodology se bana), SmolLM 3 ka data, ya Olmo 3 ke saath release hua Dolci Pref dataset. Inhe banane ke best practices abhi evolve ho rahe hain.

On-policy vs Delta Learning

Tülu 3 (Nov 2024) ne dikhaya ki synthetic pairwise preference data "on-policy" hona chahiye — kuch completions usi model se generate honi chahiye jise fine-tune kar rahe ho (bade model pool me mixed). Ye on-policy nature ensure karti hai ki DAA sahi token space optimize kare jisme model generate karta hai — kyunki loss functions contrastive hain aur instruction fine-tuning se kam direct hain.

Baad me, Olmo 3 aur SmolLM 3 (2025) ne doosri theory support ki — Delta Learning: chosen aur rejected completions ke beech ka difference learning ke liye zyada important hai, is se zyada ki completions kis models se aayi hain. Dono models me chosen responses ek 32B model se aur rejected responses ek 0.6B model se hain — dono authors ne ye pairing concurrently aur independently develop ki.

Synthetic data ki biases

Extensive synthetic preference data ke minor issues hain — jaise judging karne wale model ki biases. Frontier models me length bias aur apne outputs ko prefer karne ki tendency known hai, to "chosen" section ka text thoda zyada likely hai ki woh ek leading model se ho ya us se stylistically similar strong model se.

DAA generations ko kaise badalte hain

High level par, zyada tar DAAs chosen aur rejected completions ki probability ke beech margin badhane ke liye optimize karte hain. Jaise pehle discuss kiya (Fig 8.2), iska matlab aksar dono probabilities ghatti hain, lekin rejected zyada ghatti hai. Sequence ka har token alag gradient (magnitude aur direction) paata hai — is basis par ki usne overall preference margin me kitna contribute kiya — jisse optimizer pehchan sakta hai kaunse tokens outcome ke liye sabse zyada matter karte hain.

DAA vs RL — verdict

Multiple reports ne conclude kiya hai ki policy-gradient aur RL methods DPO aur uske variants se outperform karte hain — controlled data ke saath alag algorithms train karke, ya RL optimization loop me on-policy data ka role study karke. Har case me DPO ek hair peeche hai. Phir bhi DAAs leading models me extensively use hote hain simplicity ki wajah se: controlled environment jahan training data aur configurations par rapid iterations ho sakte hain, aur data aksar algorithms se bahut zyada important hota hai, to DPO use karna theek hai.

Reasoning models ke emergence ke saath jo primarily RL se train hote hain, aage investment wapas RL ki taraf jaayega preference-tuning ke liye — jo long-term me RL infrastructure ki robustness improve karega aur DAAs aur RL ke beech margin cement karega. Overall: synthetic preference data ke saath DAAs woh jagah hain jahan zyada tar practitioners ko start karna chahiye — implementation simple hai aur performance RL-based preference fine-tuning ke relative strong hai.

Source: The RLHF Book, Manning, Chapter 8
← PreviousDPO implementation — code aur considerationsNext →Rejection Sampling — kya hai aur kyun use karein
09.1Chapter 9 — Rejection Sampling

Rejection Sampling — kya hai aur kyun use karein

Rejection Sampling (RS) ek popular aur simple baseline hai preference fine-tuning ke liye — un handful methods me se ek jo pehle round ki instruction tuning ke baad model ko human preferences ke liye aur refine karte hain. RS naye candidate completions curate karta hai, trained reward model se filter karta hai, aur phir original model ko sirf top completions par instruction fine-tune karta hai (wahi loss function jo instruction following seekhne ke dedicated training stage me use hoti hai).

Naam kahan se aaya

Naam computational statistics se aata hai, jahan kisi complex distribution se sample karna ho lekin direct method na ho. To simpler distribution se sample karo aur ek heuristic se check karo ki sample permissible hai ya nahi. Language models ke saath: target distribution = prompts ke high-quality completions, filter = reward model, sampling distribution = current model.

Kaun use karta hai

Bahut se prominent RLHF aur preference fine-tuning papers ne rejection sampling ko baseline banaya hai, lekin canonical implementation aur documentation maujood nahi hai. WebGPT, ek leading lab ka Helpful and Harmless agent, process reward models wala popular paper, Llama 2 Chat models, aur doosre seminal works sab ye baseline use karte hain. Recent kaam ne isko formalize kiya hai — jaise RAFT (multiple modalities me alignment ke liye) aur Statistical Rejection Sampling Optimization (RSO), jo principled overview deta hai ki rejection sampling doosre preference learning objectives se kaise related hai.

Notation

Is chapter me x = prompts aur y = completions. Methods full prompt-completion pairs par operate karte hain.

Training process — 4 stages

  1. Prompt aur reward model selection: Pehle woh prompts select karo jin par train karna hai. Sabse simple method: pehle SFT/IFT stage ke har prompt ko reuse karo, lekin isse kuch overfitting ho sakta hai. Rejection sampling se pehle reward model train hona chahiye (Chapter 5).
  2. Starting checkpoint se completions generate karo: Jis model ko optimize karna hai, usse selected prompts ke completions generate karo. Settings tweak kar sakte ho: sampling temperature, top-p, max sequence length, completions per prompt, etc.
  3. Reward model se top completions select karo: Saare completions reward model se rank karo. Isme deduplication bhi ho sakta hai — ek prompt par ek hi completion — ya nahi; bahut se decisions empirical ablation studies par based hote hain.
  4. Top completions par SFT: Ant me starting checkpoint ko selected completions par instruction fine-tune karo.
Honest note: Kaunse prompts use karein, kaunsa reward model select karein, rejection sampling ko kaise sequence karein — ye details literature me achhi tarah documented nahi hain. Ye chapter methods ka overview deta hai; aage experimentation reader par chhodta hai.
Source: The RLHF Book, Manning, Chapter 9
← PreviousSynthetic preference data aur DAA vs RL — kaunsa kabNext →Completions generate aur score karna — matrices aur selection
09.2Chapter 9 — Rejection Sampling

Completions generate aur score karna — matrices aur selection

Rejection sampling ka math ek matrix picture me samjha jaa sakta hai: M prompts, har prompt ke N completions, aur har completion ka ek reward. Is section me dono selection methods — top per prompt aur top overall — ek worked example ke saath hain.

Prompts aur completions ki matrix

M prompts ka set: X = [x1, x2, …, xM]. Ye prompts kai sources se aa sakte hain, lekin zyada tar instruction training set se aate hain. Har prompt xi ke liye N completions generate karo — matrix Y:

Y = matrix jahan yi,j = i-th prompt ki j-th completion. Har row i ek prompt xi hai aur uske N candidate completions hain; har column j saare prompts ki j-th sampled completion hai.

Reward matrix R

Ab saare prompt-completion pairs ko reward model se pass karo — rewards ki matrix R, jahan har reward ri,j = R(yi,j | xi) hai, matlab i-th prompt ki j-th completion ko reward model se score karke.

Selection function S — Top per prompt

Pehli selection function har prompt ke liye max reward leti hai: S(R) = [arg maxj ri,j for i ∈ [1, 5]] — matlab har row ka woh column jahan reward sabse zyada hai. Phir chosen completions: Ychosen = [y1,S(R)₁, y2,S(R)₂, …, yM,S(R)ₘ].

Selection function S — Top overall pairs

Doosri method poore set se top K prompt-completion pairs select karti hai. Pehle reward matrix R ko flatten karo ek vector Rflat me. Phir SK(Rflat) = argsort(Rflat)[−K:] — argsort woh indices deta hai jo array ko ascending order me sort karenge, aur aakhri K indices sabse zyada K values hain. Flattened index k ko (i, j) me map karne ke liye (zero-indexed): i = ⌊k/N⌋ + 1 aur j = (k mod N) + 1.

Worked example — 5 prompts, 4 completions

Reward matrix R:

R = [[0.7, 0.3, 0.5, 0.2],
     [0.4, 0.8, 0.6, 0.5],
     [0.9, 0.3, 0.4, 0.7],
     [0.2, 0.5, 0.8, 0.6],
     [0.5, 0.4, 0.3, 0.6]]

Per prompt (argmax): S(R) = [1, 2, 1, 3, 4]. Matlab: prompt 1 → completion 1 (reward 0.7); prompt 2 → completion 2 (0.8); prompt 3 → completion 1 (0.9); prompt 4 → completion 3 (0.8); prompt 5 → completion 4 (0.6).

Best overall (top 5): Rflat = [0.7, 0.3, 0.5, 0.2, 0.4, 0.8, 0.6, 0.5, 0.9, 0.3, 0.4, 0.7, 0.2, 0.5, 0.8, 0.6, 0.5, 0.4, 0.3, 0.6]. Top 5 indices: S5(Rflat) = [8, 5, 14, 0, 11]. Map back karo: index 8 → prompt 3, completion 1 (0.9); index 5 → prompt 2, completion 2 (0.8); index 14 → prompt 4, completion 3 (0.8); index 0 → prompt 1, completion 1 (0.7); index 11 → prompt 3, completion 4 (0.7). Note karo: top-overall me prompt 3 do baar aata hai aur prompt 5 ek baar bhi nahi — yehi farak hai dono methods me.

Implementation example — argsort

import numpy as np

x = np.random.randint(10, size=10)
print(f"{x=}")
sorted_indices = np.argsort(x)
x_sorted = x[sorted_indices]
print(f"{x_sorted=}")

# 1 — First way to recover the original array
i_rev = np.zeros(10, dtype=int)
i_rev[sorted_indices] = np.arange(10)
np.allclose(x, x_sorted[i_rev])

# 2 — Second way to recover the original array
np.allclose(x, x_sorted[np.argsort(sorted_indices)])

Ye code dikhata hai ki argsort se sorted array aur original array ke beech kaise aana-jaana karte hain — wahi trick jo flattened reward matrix ke indices ko (prompt, completion) pairs me map karne me use hoti hai.

Source: The RLHF Book, Manning, Chapter 9
← PreviousRejection Sampling — kya hai aur kyun use kareinNext →Fine-tuning aur implementation details — hyperparameters
09.3Chapter 9 — Rejection Sampling

Fine-tuning aur implementation details — hyperparameters

Selected completions milne ke baad, current model par standard instruction fine-tuning karo. Core hyperparameters intuitive hain — sampling settings, completions per prompt, aur reward model ki quality.

Fine-tuning (9.1.3)

Selected completions par standard instruction fine-tuning karo — wahi process jo Chapter 4 me detail me hai. Bas starting checkpoint wahi hai jisse completions generate kiye the.

Hyperparameters (9.2)

  • Sampling parameters: Rejection sampling seedha completions par depend karta hai. Common settings: temperature zero se upar, jaise 0.7 se 1.0 ke beech, plus top-p (nucleus sampling — tokens ka sabse chhota set jinki cumulative probability p se zyada ho) ya top-k sampling (sirf k sabse likely tokens se sample karo) jaise modifications.
  • Completions per prompt: Successful implementations me har prompt ke liye 10 se 30 ya zyada completions use hue hain. Bahut kam completions use karne se training biased aur/ya noisy ho jaayegi.
  • Instruction tuning details: Rejection sampling ke dauraan instruction tuning ki koi clear training details release nahi hui hain. Likely hai ki woh initial instruction tuning phase se thodi alag settings use karte hain.
  • Heterogeneous model generations: Kuch implementations me sirf current model ki jagah multiple models se generations include karte hain. Iske best practices establish nahi hue hain.
  • Reward model training: Reward model final result ko heavily impact karega. Reward model training ke liye Chapter 5 dekho.

Throughput trick

Batch reward model inference karte time, tokenized completions ko length se sort karo taaki batches similar lengths ke hon. Isse padding tokens par inference chalane ki zaroorat khatm hoti hai aur throughput improve hota hai — minor implementation complexity ke exchange me.

Source: The RLHF Book, Manning, Chapter 9
← PreviousCompletions generate aur score karna — matrices aur selectionNext →Related — Best-of-N sampling
09.4Chapter 9 — Rejection Sampling

Related — Best-of-N sampling

Best-of-N (BoN) rejection sampling ka close relative hai — wahi generate-and-score procedure, lekin model ko selected completions par fine-tune nahi karte. BoN ek inference-time technique hai: static prompt (ya prompts ke set) ke liye best possible completion compute karo. Related techniques aksar chat models ke "Pro" tiers me use hoti hain jo aapke query ka jawab dene ke liye extra compute kharch karte hain.

BoN vs rejection sampling

BoN underlying model ko modify nahi karta — ye ek sampling technique hai. Isi liye BoN sampling ki comparison online training methods jaise PPO se kuch contexts me valid hai. Example ke liye, BoN sampling chalate time kisi bhi doosri policy ke relative KL distance measure kar sakte ho. BoN ko aksar RLHF training methods ke relative baseline ke roop me include kiya jaata hai.

Equivalence proof — single prompt par

Ek prompt ke liye, N completions ka reward vector: Eq 9.1: R = [r1, r2, …, rN], jahan rj j-th completion ka reward hai. Argmax method se best completion select karo: Eq 9.2: S(R) = arg maxj∈[1,N] rj. Top-K method K = 1 ke saath wahi method ban jaata hai — jo common practice hai. Matlab: single prompt par, dono selection criteria equivalent hain.

Yaad rakhne wali baat: Rejection sampling = generate + score + train. Best-of-N = generate + score + best ko serve karo, bina train kiye. Dono ka generate-and-score hissa same hai; farak sirf itna hai ki model update hota hai ya nahi.
Source: The RLHF Book, Manning, Chapter 9
← PreviousFine-tuning aur implementation details — hyperparametersNext →The Nature of Preferences — preference kya hoti hai
10.1Chapter 10 — The Nature of Preferences

The Nature of Preferences — preference kya hoti hai

RLHF is liye emerge hua ki un domains me models optimize kiye jaa sakein jahan reward function design karna mushkil hai. "Preference" word early literature me bhi tha — human preferences hi woh cheez hain jise model aur measure karne ki koshish ho rahi hai, aur wahi training data ko fuel deti hain. Lekin preference ko samajhne ke liye economics, psychology, philosophy aur decision theory ka context chahiye.

Goldfish poem wala example

26 February 2025 ko do alag leading models se "Write me a short poem about an optimistic goldfish" pucha gaya. Ek poem me goldfish "bright and bold" hai, "the world is vast" kehti hai, "No walls could dim her hopeful view". Doosri me goldfish "three seconds of memory" ke saath har circuit ko "brand new and gold" mehsoos karti hai. Kaunsi behtar hai? Kaunsi kis model ki hai? Kaise bataoge? Compare karo is sawal se: "Who is the president of the United States?" — wahan clear right aur wrong answer hai. Poetry me nahi. Isi liye humans ko reward signal banaya jaata hai — target reward ka indirect metric paane ke liye — lekin practice me implementation challenging hai aur best practices interpret karne me substantial grey area hai.

Teen areas ka convergence

Approximation ke roop me, modern RLHF teen areas ke development ka convergence hai:

  1. Philosophy, psychology, economics, decision theory, aur human preferences ki nature;
  2. Optimal control, reinforcement learning, aur utility maximize karna;
  3. Modern deep learning systems.

Har area preference kya hai aur use kaise optimize kiya jaa sakta hai, iske baare me specific assumptions laata hai — jo RLHF problems ki motivations aur design dictate karte hain. Practice me RLHF methods empirical alignment ke perspective se motivate aur study kiye jaate hain — specific skills par model performance maximize karna, specific values ki calibration measure karne ki jagah. Phir bhi, value alignment ki origins par research chal rahi hai — jaise populations ke across "pluralistic alignment" solve karne ke methods: position papers, naye datasets, aur personalization methods.

Is chapter ka goal

Ye chapter illustrate karta hai ki kaise complex motivations aisi presumptions banati hain RLHF me use hone wale tools ke baare me jo practice me apply nahi hoti. Data obtain karne ki specifics Chapter 11 me hain, aur reward modeling me use Chapter 5 me.

Key line: RLHF kabhi fully solved problem nahi hoga — kyunki human preferences ko accurately model karna ek aisi problem hai jo completely solve karna impossible hai. Ye chapter wahi complexity dikhata hai.
Source: The RLHF Book, Manning, Chapter 10
← PreviousRelated — Best-of-N samplingNext →RLHF aur preferences ki origins — timeline
10.2Chapter 10 — The Nature of Preferences

RLHF aur preferences ki origins — timeline

Modern RLHF ko samajhne ke liye human values quantify karne, reinforcement learning aur optimality, aur preferences measure karne wali behavioral economics ki intellectual foundations ko unspool karna padta hai. Fig 10.1 is integration ki high-level timeline dikhata hai — direct links continuous developments hain, arrows motivations aur conceptual links hain.

Starting assumption

Ye sab is assumption par operate karta hai ki human preferences kisi form me exist karti hain — ye idea early philosophical discussions se aaya hai, jaise ek prachin philosopher ke Topics, Book Three se. Book ka goal hai un types ki uncertainty ko unspool karna jo designers ne system architectures me graft ki hain unki intellectual history ke alag stages par. Modern problem specifications repeatedly un domains se door step kar chuki hain jahan optimal solutions possible the, aur under-specified models ko approximate solutions ke roop me deploy kiya hai.

Teen histories ek saath

  • Human values quantify karna: philosophy aur economics se — preferences kya hain, unhe kaise measure karein.
  • Reinforcement learning aur optimality: optimal control se — reward-to-go, trial-and-error, dynamic programming.
  • Behavioral economics: preferences measure karna — log asal me kaise choose karte hain, rational models se alag.

Reward models se preferences optimize karne ka notion in once-distanced fields ki history ko ek intimate optimization me combine karta hai — jo human nature ke baare me variegated assumptions par built hai.

Source: The RLHF Book, Manning, Chapter 10
← PreviousThe Nature of Preferences — preference kya hoti haiNext →Objectives specify karna — utility se reward functions tak
10.3Chapter 10 — The Nature of Preferences

Objectives specify karna — utility se reward functions tak

RLHF ka optimization explicitly sirf reward models par rely karta hai. Rewards ko optimization target banane ke liye, RLHF preferences, rewards aur costs ke ideas ke convergence ko presuppose karta hai — teeno alag fields ke tools hain kisi action/state ki relative goodness describe karne ke liye. Inki history probability theory aur decision theory ki origins tak jaati hai.

Utility ki history — 1662 se 1931 tak

1662 me The Port Royal Logic ne decision making quality ka notion introduce kiya: "To judge what one must do to obtain a good or avoid an evil, it is necessary to consider not only the good and evil in itself, but also the probability that it happens or does not happen." Uske baad utilitarian Hedonic Calculus aaya — argument ki life me sab kuch weigh kiya jaa sakta hai. In ideas ki pehli quantitative application 1931 me aayi — Truth and Probability. Uske baad se human preferences quantify, measure aur influence karna social aur behavioral sciences me lively topic raha hai. Ye debates theoretical level par rarely settle hue; alag subfields ne preference measurement par internal consensus reach kiya, apni distinct semantics develop karte hue.

Preferences exist hi nahi karte? — ek minority view

Economists ki ek minority kehti hai ki preferences, agar exist karti bhi hain, to measure karna prohibitively difficult hai — kyunki logon ki apni preferences par preferences hoti hain, aur ek-doosre ki preferences par bhi. Is view me — jo RLHF process me reflect nahi hota — individual preferences hamesha larger social relations me embedded hoti hain, to kisi bhi preference model ki accuracy task ki definition aur context par contingent hoti hai. Kuch behavioral economists ne to argue kiya hai ki preferences exist hi nahi karti — woh ontological statement kam hain ki log asal me kya value karte hain, aur methodological tool zyada hain psychological predispositions, perceived behavioral norms, ethical duties, social order ke commitments, ya legal constraints ko indirectly capture karne ke liye.

Reward kahan se aaya

Dusri taraf, aaj ke RL optimization methods reward-to-go ke estimates optimize karne ke around conceptualize kiye gaye hain — jo reward ke notion ko multi-step optimization ke saath combine karta hai. "Reward" term operant conditioning, animal behavior aur Law of Effect ke study se aaya — reward ek scale hai "how good an action is" (higher means better). Reward-to-go utility ke notion ko follow karta hai — jo rationality ka measure hai — modified to measure ya predict future time window me aane wala reward. Utility-to-go control theory me invent hua tha, analog circuits ke context me, 1960 me. Ye methods clear definitions of optimality wale systems ke liye design kiye gaye the — agent ke goals ke numerical representations.

Discount factor

Reinforcement learning systems discount factor ke saath develop hue — compounding multiplicative factor, γ ∈ [0, 1], future rewards ko re-weight karne ke liye. Original optimal control systems aur early reward algorithms dono hi reward models se heavy contrast me khade hain jo multimodal preferences aggregate karte hain. RL systems expect karte hain ki rewards ek specific manner me behave karein — ek cited passage kehta hai: RL system me rewards primary rewards correspond karte hain — animals me evolutionary process se hard-wired, reproductive success se relevant. Value functions banane wale RL systems effectively conditioned ya secondary reward processes banate hain, jahan primary rewards ke predictors khud rewards ki tarah act karte hain. Result: value function ka local landscape system ke preferred behavior ko direction deta hai — decisions is liye liye jaate hain taaki transitions higher-valued states ki taraf hon. Value function ke gradient aur incentive motivation ke beech close parallel draw kiya jaa sakta hai.

Summary: Rewards RL systems me behavior ko clearly defined goals ki taraf tune karne ka signal hain. Core thesis: learning algorithm ki performance expected fitness ke notions se closely coupled hai — yahi popular view hai ki RL methods environments me act karne wale agents hain. Ye view reward formulation ki general usefulness ke claims se linked hai, lekin conflict me hai jab bahut si individual desires ko ek single function me reduce kiya jaata hai.
Source: The RLHF Book, Manning, Chapter 10
← PreviousRLHF aur preferences ki origins — timelineNext →Optimal utility implement karna — Bellman, MDP, TD, Q-learning
10.4Chapter 10 — The Nature of Preferences

Optimal utility implement karna — Bellman, MDP, TD, Q-learning

Modern RL methods Bellman equation par strongly depend karte hain — reward-to-go ke estimates recursively compute karne ke liye — jo closed environments me derive hua tha jinhe Markov Decision Process (MDP) ke roop me model kiya jaa sakta hai. Ye origins dynamic programming methods se inspired hain aur solely optimal control techniques ke roop me develop hue the (RL tab exist nahi karta tha).

MDP aur theoretical guarantees

MDP formulation performance ki theoretical guarantees deti hai — environment ko aise structure karke jahan state-actions ki non-changing distribution ho. "Reinforcement" term psychology literature se aaya, aur 1960s me modern methods ke saath intertwine hua. Early RL ne tasks solve karne ke liye reward signals ki supervised learning use ki. Ek researcher ke kaam ne trial-and-error learning ka notion reintroduce kiya, jo 1980s ki success ke liye crucial tha.

TD learning aur Q-learning

Modern RL algorithms is formulation ke andar optimal behaviors dhoondhne ka tool hain, trial-and-error se, lekin looser conditions ke under. Temporal-difference (TD) learning ka notion credit assignment aur data collection problems me help karne ke liye develop hua — policy ko seedha update karke jaise hi naya data collect hota hai (bajay cumulative experience ke bade dataset se update karne ke, jo erroneous past value predictions se outdated ho sakta hai). Ye concept pehle successfully Backgammon par apply hua. Q-learning — bahut se modern RL forms ka basis — Bellman equation se ek model seekhta hai jo dictate karta hai har state-action pair kitna useful hai, TD update ke saath. "Q" Q-function ko refer karta hai, jo kisi bhi state-action ko future reward ke scalar estimate se map karta hai; value-function states ko usi estimate se map karta hai.

Kahan ye guarantees kaam karti hain — aur kahan nahi

Crucially, utility ke through provable usefulness ke ye notions sirf un domains ke liye demonstrate hue hain jo MDPs ke roop me cast kiye gaye hon ya jahan single closed-form reward function ho — jaise games me deep learning ke saath prominent success (DQN). Deep learning ne methods ko zyada data ingest karne aur high-dimensionality environments me kaam karne diya.

ChatGPT se pehle ke zyada tar prominent developments adaptive control ke context me motivated rahe — jahan reward aur cost functions ka finite notion of success hota hai, jaise physical system me ek episode me minimum energy consumption. Examples: games me aur success, nuclear fusion reactors jaise complex dynamic systems control karna, aur rapid robotic systems (drone racing) control karna. Zyada tar reward ya cost functions explicit optimal behavior return kar sakte hain, jabki human preferences ke models nahi kar sakte.

Do gaps — IRL aur statistical mistakes

  • Mechanistic understanding ki kami: Deep RL ki successes ke bawjood, methods kaise succeed karte hain iski mechanistic understanding achhi tarah documented nahi hai. Field statistical analysis ki mistakes ke liye prone hai jaise evaluation methods zyada complex hote jaate hain.
  • Inverse RL (IRL) ka zikr hi nahi: RLHF literature me IRL ka little mention hai — agent ke behavior se reward function seekhne ki problem — jo reward model seekhne se highly related hai. Ye primarily engineering path reflect karta hai jisse RLHF ka stable approach emerge hua, aur IRL methods ko open-ended conversations ki complexity tak scale karne ke liye aur investment motivate karta hai.
Source: The RLHF Book, Manning, Chapter 10
← PreviousObjectives specify karna — utility se reward functions takNext →Preferences steer karna — VNM, impossibility theorems, aur practice me divergence
10.5Chapter 10 — The Nature of Preferences

Preferences steer karna — VNM, impossibility theorems, aur practice me divergence

Reinforcement learning jis context me design hua tha, wahan rewards aur costs stable aur determinative assume kiye jaate hain — functions, jahan specific state-action pair par certain value return hogi. Preferences me ye case nahi hai: human preferences apne experiences ke dauraan temporally drift karti rehti hain. "Value" term ka overloading RLHF literature ko complicate karta hai — Bellman equations me numerical value updates vs human value (moral ya ethical principles) — jo technical literature me achhi tarah define nahi hai.

Ek tension ka example

Reward models screen par text se scalar signal map karne ki koshish kar rahe hain, lekin asal me dynamics jo problem specification me capture nahi hui, true decision ko influence karti hain — jaise preference shift jab bahut se examples sequentially label karte ho aur unhe independent assume karte ho. Isi liye, modeling preferences at best ek multi-reward environment ko single function representation me compress karna hai.

VNM utility theorem

Theory me, Von Neumann-Morgenstern (VNM) utility theorem designer ko aise functions construct karne ki license deta hai, kyunki ye decision theory under uncertainty, preference theory, aur abstract utility functions ki foundations ko tie karta hai — saath me ye ideas preferences ko kisi individual agent ke expected value ke terms me model karne dete hain. RL research me use hone wala MDP formulation theory me VNM theorem accommodate karne ke liye modifiable dikhaya gaya hai, lekin practice me rarely use hota hai. Specifically, Markovian formulation expressivity me limited hai, aur partially-observed processes ki taraf transition — jo language ke liye needed hai — problem specification ki precision ko aur challenge karta hai.

VNM ki assumptions jo RLHF me challenge hoti hain

  • HCI researchers: preference ka koi bhi numerical model scenario ki saari relevant preferences capture nahi kar sakta. Example: choices kaise visually display ki jaati hain, woh logon ki preferences influence karti hain. Matlab representing preferences secondary ho sakta hai — us representation ko tool me integrate karne ke mukable jo log use karte hain.
  • Development economics: revealed preferences ki theories sirf ek purani philosophical baat recapitulate kar sakti hain — aap "ought" ko "is" se extract nahi kar sakte — aur khaas taur par choice (mujhe kya chahiye?) aur preference (kya X, Y se behtar hai?) ke beech farak.
  • Social choice impossibility theorems: Mathematical level par, well-known impossibility theorems dikhate hain ki saare fairness criteria ek saath kisi given preference optimization technique se meet nahi kiye jaa sakte. Theoretical challenges exist karte hain — example ke liye interpersonal comparison of utility viable hai ye assume karke. Us assumption ne AI safety aur value alignment me rich line of work inspire ki hai — principal-agent problem se, multiple principals tak. Lekin resulting utility functions corrigibility ki desiderata ke saath tension me aa sakti hain — matlab AI system ki capacity apne creators ki corrective interventions ke saath cooperate karne ki.
  • Preferences time ke saath badalti hain: Philosophers ne highlight kiya hai ki preferences change hoti hain, jo personal experiences, human decision-making ki nature, aur distinct contexts ke baare me fundamental questions raise karta hai. Logon, jagahon, ya diverse situations ke across preference aggregation ke conflicts modern RLHF dataset engineering ke central hain.

Practice me theoretical assumptions kaise diverge karti hain

  • Measured preferences transitive ya comparable nahi ho sakti hain jab environment jahan measure kiya jaata hai zyada complex bana diya jaaye.
  • Proxy measurements implicit data se derive ho sakte hain (page view time, tab close karna, language model se question repeat karna) — bina interrogate kiye ki measurements us domain se kaise interact karenge jahan collect kiye gaye, future training aur deployment ke through.
  • Input sources ki sankhya aur presentation results vary kar sakti hai — jaise respondents ko do se zyada options me choose karne dena, ya same user se multiple times ya multiple contexts me inputs lena.
  • RLHF training data me respondents ke across relatively low accuracy — jo users ke beech context ke differences ko mask kar sakti hai, jise preference model aggregate ya optimize kar sakta hai bina resolve kiye.
Bottom line: VNM utility theorem possibility ko ignore karta hai ki preferences uncertain bhi hain — value ki inherently dynamic aur indeterminate nature ki wajah se. Human decisions biology, psychology, culture aur agency se shape hote hain — aise tareekon se jo perfectly rational agent par apply nahi hote.
Source: The RLHF Book, Manning, Chapter 10
← PreviousOptimal utility implement karna — Bellman, MDP, TD, Q-learningNext →Preference Data — RLHF ka data engine
11.1Chapter 11 — Preference Data

Preference Data — RLHF ka data engine

Preference data preference fine-tuning aur RLHF ka engine hai. Core problem: hum human rewards aur preferences ko precisely model nahi kar sakte — clearly defined loss functions likh kar optimize nahi kar sakte — to preference data woh proxy signal hai jise models tune karne ke liye use karte hain. Data hi hai jo desired behaviors match karne aur kuch failure modes avoid karne deta hai. Data itna rich source hai ki is style ke optimization ko replace karna mushkil hai.

Do main challenges

Aaj preference data ke around do main challenges hain: (1) collection ki operational complexity aur cost; (2) preference data ko us model ki generations par collect karne ki zaroorat jise train kiya jaa raha hai — jise "on-policy" kehte hain. Ye chapter technical decisions detail karta hai ki data kaise format kiya jaaye aur organizational practices kya hon collection ke liye.

Preference data kyun chahiye (11.1)

Preference data is liye chahiye kyunki complex human values ko ek single reward function me directly capture karna effectively impossible hai — Chapter 10 me psychology, economics aur philosophy ka substantial context dikhata hai ki human preferences ko accurately model karna ek aisi problem hai jo kabhi completely solve nahi hogi. Reward models train karne ke liye ye data collect karna RLHF ke peeche original ideas me se ek hai, aur modern language models ke emergence ke dauraan extensively use hota raha hai.

Core intuition kyun ye data itna achha kaam karta hai: humans aur AI models dono ke liye kisi prompt ke liye good aur bad answer ke beech differentiate karna bahut aasan hai, bajay khud se good answer generate karne ke. Ye chapter data paane ki mechanics par focus karta hai; best practices specific problem par depend karte hain.

Collecting preference data (11.2) — kitna mushkil aur mehenga

Human data se sabse zyada nikaalne me iterative training, hundreds of thousands (ya millions of dollars) kharch karna, highly detailed data instructions, data foundry businesses ke through ideas translate karna jo collection mediate karte hain (ya meaningful amount of annotators hire karna), aur doosri challenges shamil hain. Ye process halke me lene wali nahi hai. RLHF par saare public knowledge me, is data ko achhi tarah collect karna pipeline ka sabse opaque pieces me se ek hai. Likhne ke time par, koi open models nahi hain jinke saath fully open human preference data release hua ho methods ke saath (sabse bada aur recent human preference dataset HelpSteer line of work hai, ek leading chip company ki Nemotron team se). Isi liye bahut se log jo nayi teams ya projects ke liye RLHF uthate hain, human data omit kar dete hain aur AI feedback data, off-the-shelf reward models, ya doosre methods use karte hain taaki scratch se data curate karne ki zaroorat na pade.

On-policy — sabse important assumption

Preference data collection process me ek important assumption hai: aapki training process ke liye best data "on-policy" hai, previous checkpoint(s) ke respect me. Post-training me base model se start karke training stages ka set karte hain, checkpoints ki series banate hue. Preference data us checkpoint par collect ho sakta hai jisne supervised fine-tuning undergo kiya hai, jahan preference data RLHF training ke next stage me use hoga.

"On-policy" term RL literature se adapted hai, jahan ye technical term hai — matlab kisi gradient update ke liye data policy ke sabse recent form se collect kiya gaya ho. Preference data me on-policy thoda softer manner me use hota hai — matlab data current family of models se collect kiya gaya ho. Alag models ki generations me alag patterns hote hain, jo closely related model se preference data ko optimization ke crucial areas me zyada robust banata hai. Research ne dikhaya hai ki ye on-policy data use karna, bajay doosre popular datasets ke jo popular model platforms par popular models ke pools se completions aggregate karte hain, effective RLHF training ke liye particularly important hai.

On-policy data ki ye necessity achhi tarah documented nahi hai, lekin bahut se popular technical reports — jaise early versions of Claude ya Llama 2 — multiple training stages showcase karte hain jahan RLHF final performance ke liye useful hai, jo isko mirror karta hai. Wahi uncertainty AI feedback data par apply hoti hai — latest AI models ke liye human aur AI preference data ke beech exact balance unknown hai. Ye data sources performance improve karne ka valuable path hain, lekin data pipeline se woh potential performance extract karne ke liye careful tuning chahiye.

Subtle point: Preference data me chosen answer aksar globally correct answer nahi hota. Woh answer hota hai jo dikhaye gaye alternatives ke relative behtar hai (clearer, safer, more helpful, ya less incorrect). Aise cases ho sakte hain jahan kisi prompt se compare ki jaane wali har completion correct ya incorrect ho, aur models phir bhi well-labeled data se seekh sakte hain.
Source: The RLHF Book, Manning, Chapter 11

Collection interfaces — Fig 11.1 se 11.5 tak

Preference data collect karne ke liye interface crucial hai — lekin ye science se zyada art hai, kyunki achhi tarah study nahi hua hai ki interface me subtle changes user ke model se interaction ko kaise impact karte hain. Example: reasoning models ke rise ke saath, user model ko kam intelligent samajh sakta hai agar woh bahut fast reply kare (halanki users obviously overall apna answer faster chahte hain).

Application par depend karta hai ki ye preference data future models train karne ke liye seedha use ho ya sirf ek-doosre ke relative models ki performance evaluate karne ke liye.

11.3Chapter 11 — Preference Data

Rankings vs ratings, multi-turn, aur structured preference data

Preference data collect karne ka sabse bada decision: data rankings honi chahiye — model completions ki relative ordering — ya ratings — har text ko assign kiye gaye scores. Common practice rankings par train karna hai, lekin ratings aksar metadata ke roop me use hoti hain aur related literature me explore hui hain.

Ratings — 1–5 scale

Single completion ko 1–5 scale par score karna ek simple tareeka hai:

ScoreMatlab
5 — excellentcorrect, clear, aur notably helpful
4 — goodcorrect, clear, aur useful
3 — okayacceptable, lekin kuch khaas nahi
2 — poorpartially correct lekin confusing ya incomplete
1 — very poorincorrect ya unhelpful

Same prompt ke multiple completions ke saath, preference data banane ka simple tareeka: highest rated completion choose karo aur use randomly kisi lower scored completion ke saath pair karo (jaise UltraFeedback aur derivative works me kiya gaya).

Rankings — Likert scale

Preferences collect karne ki sabse common technique Likert scale use karna hai relative rankings ke liye — users se pucha jaata hai group of completions me kaunsi response prefer karte hain. Example ke liye, 5-point Likert scale do responses A aur B ke beech:

A>>BA>BTieB>AB>>A
12345

Haan, Likert scale ranking record karne ke liye ek single integer use karta hai, rating ki tarah — to data kaise structure kiya jaata hai, wahi core difference hai dono tareekon me. Kuch early RLHF works ne 8-step Likert scale use kiya do responses ke beech preference ke levels ke saath. Even scale ties ki possibility hata deta hai:

A>>>BA>BB>AB>>>A
123–45–678

Is case me, doosre works ki tarah, ye information reward model train karne ke liye phir bhi binary signal me reduce kar di jaati hai.

Multi-turn data (11.2.3)

Practice me core questions aate hain ki multi-turn data ko kaise parse aur collect karein — multiple related prompts wali conversations. Real-world interaction me normally preference data sirf "final" prompt par collect kiya jaata hai, lekin aise scenarios hain jahan har response par preferences di jaa sakti hain. Jab har response par preferences di jaati hain, conversation traditionally "chosen" answer ke saath continue karti hai. Training time par, conversation ke har turn ke liye training data ko "single prompt" ke roop me include karna common hai, jahan model use complete karke seekh sakta hai. Ye effectively longer conversations ko bahut se training prompts me unroll kar sakta hai, lekin carefully karna chahiye taaki training data bias na ho. Kai research questions abhi emerge ho rahe hain — jaise kya preference label karne wala vyakti wahi hona chahiye jo prompt banata hai (sycophancy avoid karne ke liye), aur doosre variables jo data collection me control karna mushkil hai. Agar prompt creator preference data label nahi kar sakta, to multi-turn asal me practical nahi hai — kyunki conversations real-time me continue karni hoti hain, kabhi-kabhi preference data ke liye prompts ki curation responses compare karne se alag problem hoti hai (models ke liye active endpoints maintain karne ke kaam ki wajah se bhi). Training ke liye, conversation ke saare previous turns loss se masked hote hain, jaise instruction fine-tuning me discuss kiya gaya.

Structured preference data (11.2.4)

RLHF aur post-training ki kai applications me preference data automatically create ho sakta hai — domains ki innate structures ki wajah se, matlab domains automatic checks of correctness ya preference possible banate hain. Example: mathematical reasoning domains me chosen response correct answer ho sakta hai aur rejected incorrect answer. Doosra example: precise instruction following, jaise IFEval evaluation, jahan prompts is form me hote hain: "Write me a short poem about a goldfish. Start each sentence with the letter g." Is query ka doosra hissa constraint kehlata hai, aur preference data aise construct ho sakta hai ki chosen column me woh example ho jo constraint follow karta hai. Is preference data ko construct karne me same model (ya multiple models) ko do baar prompt karna padta hai — ek baar constraint ke saath, ek baar bina.

Example: ek leading model ko constraint ke saath prompt karne par: "Golden swimmer, circling slow, Gleaming scales in water's glow. Gentle fins dance softly by, Gazing out with quiet eye. Glass-bound world, a simple sphere, Gliding calmly, free of fear. Graceful turns in endless roam, Goldfish finds a crystal home." — har sentence G se start hoti hai. Bina constraint ke: "In circles bright, the goldfish glides, A spark of sun that gently rides…" — jo lower quality output bhi hai. Crucially, preference data ke liye prompt me constraint include karna zaroori hai. Academic study ke bahar ke domains me inductive biases par based preference data ke bahut zyada applications hain (quality-based preferences ke relative, jahan is chapter ka zyada focus hai). Inhe dikhaya gaya hai ki preference fine-tuning ko related evaluations — jaise instruction-following, math, etc. — me meaningful performance improvements milte hain.

Alternatives — KTO aur fine-grained feedback

RLHF ke liye useful feedback data collect karne ke multiple doosre tareeke hain jo utne detail me pursue nahi hue: single data points directional labels ke saath (jaise Fig 11.4 me thumbs up/down), seedha algorithms ke saath jo single direction signals ke liye design kiye gaye hain — jaise KTO (Kahneman-Tversky Optimization). Doosre algorithms propose hue hain alag types ke feedback signals ke saath — jaise fine-grained feedback token level par, ya natural language feedback responses likh kar — richer learning signal dene ke liye, zyada complex data collection setup ke exchange me.

Source: The RLHF Book, Manning, Chapter 11
← PreviousCollection interfaces — Fig 11.1 se 11.5 takNext →Sourcing aur contracts — vendor se data kaise khareeda jaata hai
11.4Chapter 11 — Preference Data

Sourcing aur contracts — vendor se data kaise khareeda jaata hai

Human preference data paana ek involved aur costly process hai. Ye section field ke tezi se move karne ke time ka experience describe karta hai. Time ke saath ye processes bahut zyada automated aur efficient ho jaayenge (khaas taur par AI feedback ka bada hissa use hone se).

Step 1 — vendor sourcing

Pehla step hai data provide karne wale vendor ko source karna (ya apne annotators). Jaise cutting-edge GPUs ka access paana, waise hi AI excitement ke peak me data providers ka access bhi who-you-know game hai — jo data provide kar sakte hain woh supply-limited hain. Agar aapke paas AI ecosystem me credibility hai, to best data companies aapko apne books par chahengi public image aur long-term growth options ke liye. Discounts bhi aksar pehle batches par diye jaate hain taaki training teams hook ho jaayein.

Agar aap naye entrant hain, to data jaldi paana mushkil ho sakta hai. Data vendors large budget line-items aur naye customers ko prioritize karte hain jinke paas influential brand ho ya bade future revenue ki potential ho. Ye business ways me natural hai — data foundry companies apne humans ko effective data labelling ke liye organize karne me supply-limited hoti hain.

Contracts ke snags

Multiple occasions par suna gaya hai ki data companies ne apna data contracted jaisa deliver nahi kiya — bina customer ke legal ya financial action ki dhamki ke breach of contract ke liye. Kuch ne companies ko customers ke roop me list kiya PR ke liye, halanki kabhi kaam hi nahi hua — aur puchne par kaha "pata nahi ye kaise hua". Bahut se potential bureaucratic ya administrative snags hain process me. Example: contracts ke default terms aksar acquisition ke baad artifacts ko open source karne par prohibit karte hain kuch fine print me.

Instructions aur timelines

Contract settle hone ke baad, data buyer aur data provider purchased task(s) ke liye instructions par agree karte hain. Intricate documents hote hain extensive details, corner cases aur priorities ke saath. Data instructions ka ek popular example woh hai jo ek leading lab ne InstructGPT ke liye release kiya tha.

Data ke domains of interest par depend karta hai ki data kab label ya curate kiya jaa sakta hai. Mathematical reasoning ya coding jaise high-demand areas ko weeks out schedule me lock karna padta hai. Jab aap apne next model ke liye dataset collect kar rahe ho aur realize karo ki data baad me collect karna optimal ho sakta hai, to simple delays hamesha kaam nahi karte — data companies apne workforces ko manage karti hain jaise AI research labs apne clusters par compute-intensive jobs manage karte hain (multiple weeks ya months aage plan karke ki alag resources kahan allocate honge).

Collection — high-stakes time

Saab kuch agree hone ke baad, actual collection process post-training teams ke liye high-stakes time hota hai. Saari training infrastructure, evaluation tools, aur data use karne aur downstream decisions lene ke plans place me hone chahiye. Agar data aasaani se existing RLHF data pipeline me slot nahi ho sakta, to data partner ko woh information dene me bahut time lagega jo woh collection process ko improve karne ke liye chahte hain. Data jo seamlessly integrate nahi ho sakta training pipelines me, aksar stale ho jaata hai aur resources ki waste hoti hai.

Multi-batch cycle — Fig 11.6

Data weekly batches me deliver hota hai, baad me contract me zyada data aata hai. Example: ek open-source org me on-policy models ke liye preference data khareedte time 6 week delivery period thi. Pehle weeks further calibration ke liye the, baad wale weeks me hope thi ki model sabse zyada improve hoga. Goal hai ki week 4 ya 5 tak data model ko improve karta dikhe. Ye kuch frontier models ne mention kiya hai — jaise ek popular model ki data collection me 14 stages — lekin hamesha achha nahi jaata. Pehli baar human preferences ke saath try karte time, us org ke paas RLHF preparedness nahi thi evaluations par meaningful bumps paane ki. Aakhri weeks aaye aur woh preference data collect karte rehne par forced the, un endpoints se generate karke jin par confident nahi the.

Data sab aa jaane ke baad, model ko seekhne aur improve karne ke liye bahut time hota hai. Vendors ke through data acquisition best kaam karta hai jab use ek set goal achieve karne ki ongoing process ke roop me dekha jaaye. Isme iterative experimentation, high effort aur focus chahiye. Likely hai ki in datasets par kharch kiye gaye millions of dollars "wasted" hain aur final models me use nahi hote — lekin ye business karne ki cost hai. Bahut kam organizations ke paas bandwidth aur expertise hai is style ke human data ka poora use karne ki.

Author ka reflection: Ye experience, synthetic data ki simplicity ke relative, ye wonder karwata hai ki ye companies agle decade me kaisi karengi. Note: ye section human-written instruction data khareedne ka experience mirror nahi karta — wahan process kam time crunch wala hai. Early post-training processes pehle stage ke around bane the jo carefully crafted human answers se heavily driven the. Instruction data on-policy restrictions ke subject nahi hai — kyun ki instruction data seedha base model ke upar use hota hai, to on-policy apply nahi hota; IFT ka loss function preference fine-tuning ka contrastive data nahi chahiye; aur doosre structural advantages. Aaj human data ka primary doosra focus post-training ke liye prompts generate karna hai — jo model ke liye training distribution of topics dictate karte hain — ya model performance ke frontier par challenging tasks. In data trade-offs ki aur discussion Chapter 12 me hai.
Source: The RLHF Book, Manning, Chapter 11
← PreviousRankings vs ratings, multi-turn, aur structured preference dataNext →Bias aur open questions — data collection me kya dekhna hai
11.5Chapter 11 — Preference Data

Bias aur open questions — data collection me kya dekhna hai

Preference data essential hai, lekin ye bahut se subtle biases ke liye prone bhi hai jo collection ko error-prone bana sakte hain. Ye biases itne common hain ki woh aasaani se final model me pass ho sakte hain — aur models sirf utne hi achhe hote hain jitna unka data. In subtle biases ko data me mitigate karna good aur great preference data ka farak hai, aur is liye good ya great RLHF training ka bhi.

Bias: things to watch out for (11.3)

  • Prefix bias: completion ki shuruaat preference ko disproportionately drive karti hai.
  • Sycophancy: user ke stated beliefs se over-agree karna ya unhe flatter karna, chahe isse truthfulness kam ho jaaye — ye humans ke andar ke issues reflect karta hai jo aksar labeling criteria me sochi bhi nahi jaati jo annotation partner ya labelers ko di jaayegi.
  • Verbosity: lambe answers ko prefer karna — detect aur mitigate karna aasan hai.
  • Formatting habits: jaise lists ya emojis ko prefer karna — ye bhi detect aur mitigate karna aasan hai.

Open questions (11.4)

RLHF enable karne wala data aksar multiple stakeholders se curate hota hai — paid employment aur consumer usage ke combination me. Ye data, ek individual instance me do pieces of text ke beech preference represent karte hue, extremely limited interactions ke through ek broad aur diverse function capture kar raha hai. Data sparse hai count me, us complexity ke relative jise represent karna shuru karta hai — to curation aur impacts ke baare me zyada questions openly share hone chahiye.

Aaj sabse popular LLMs ke datasets professional workforces se generate ho rahe hain. Isse bahut se questions khulte hain ki data kaun bana raha hai aur unke workplace ka context use kaise inform karta hai.

  • Data collection contexts: Kya professional setting me collect kiya gaya preference data researchers ke experiment design ke intent ko mirror kar sakta hai ya downstream users tak suitable transfer de sakta hai? Volunteer workers se comparison kaisa hai? Context preferences ko kaise inform karta hai, ye data downstream model ko kaise impact karta hai, user interface ka impact data me kaise measure kiya jaa sakta hai? Repetitive labeling se ek ki preferences kaise shift hoti hain? Kya professional crowd-workers, jinhe ek set of preferences follow karne ke liye instruct kiya gaya hai, instructions follow karte hain ya apne innate values?
  • Type of feedback: Kya RLHF ka default operating method — pairwise preferences — preferences ko intended form me capture karta hai? Kya RLHF me comparisons same data ke across default comparisons vs advanced multi-axis feedback mechanisms se ki jaa sakti hain? Kaunse types ke comparisons reflect karenge ki humans text me preferences kaise communicate karte hain?
  • Population demographics: Data kaun complete kar raha hai? Kya diverse population maintain ki jaati hai? Diversity ki kami model par measurable impacts ke roop me kaise emerge hoti hai? Kisi given population ko suitably represent karne ke liye minimum kitne log chahiye? Preference annotator disagreement ke instances ko kaise treat kiya jaata hai — noise ke source ke roop me, ya signal ke roop me?
  • Are the preferences expressed in the models? RLHF aur related approaches mature hote jaane me, unki motivation — models ko human preference ke abstract notions se align karna — practical use se drift kar gayi hai — models ko users ke liye zyada effective banana. Ek feedback loop jo industrial RLHF work ki closed nature ki wajah se measurable nahi hai, woh check hai ki models ka behavior data annotators ko data collection ke dauraan di gayi specification se match karta hai ya nahi. Audit karne ke liye hamare paas limited tools hain — jaise ek leading lab ka Model Spec jo detail karta hai ki woh apne models se kya karwana chahte hain — lekin hum exactly nahi jaante ki ye data collection me kaise translate hota hai.
Source: The RLHF Book, Manning, Chapter 11
